little or no control over their affairs or national property. The proposal embodied in this bill is found to be in the public interest and most useful, permitting the submission of important national questions to the wisdom and judgment of the electors. subtopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OP DETERMINATE FOR INDETERMINATE REFORMATORY SENTENCES

speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 12, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.

subtopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OP DETERMINATE FOR INDETERMINATE REFORMATORY SENTENCES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OP DETERMINATE FOR INDETERMINATE REFORMATORY SENTENCES
speechtext:
The Prisons and Reformatories Act gives the court jurisdiction to impose a definite and an indeterminate term in a reformatory. The bill proposes to substitute determinate for indeterminate sentences. The several expressions relating to "indeterminate sentence" are found in eighteen sections or subsections of the act and the draftsman considers it inexpedient to amend each of such sections by a separate clause. This bill would revert to the old law of sentences for a definite period only.
The indeterminate legislation has been condemned by many judges and magistrates as inhuman and illegal. Canada's prisons at present are filled with youth, many first offenders, who have been unable to secure work. The lack of employment, by cause and effect, is one of the reasons for crime. Recently the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Ontario in Rex V. Bond, 1937 O. R., page 535, judgment of Hon. Mr. Justice Middleton, questioned and made observations on the legality of such legislation, as the provinces only had fundamentally the right of providing confinement for one year and three hundred and sixty-four days, and also condemned it on grounds of public policy. The
law has not acted as a deterrent nor is it reformative. It should be repealed because in practice it confers on officials of these institutions the right to detain those who have not influence enough to have employment awaiting them at the end of a definite period and gives to their decisions the force of statute law.
Mr. Justice Middleton has criticized the present practice. Let me read what he says, in part:
Many judges and magistrates when imposing an indeterminate sentence address the prisoner somewhat in these terms: . . . "If during this determinate term you prove yourself to be a good prisoner, and comply with the rules of the institution and show a disposition to be law-abiding, the parole board may, at the expiry of the definite term, allow you your liberty. It all depends upon yourself and your conduct as to how much, if any, of the indefinite term you may be called upon to serve."
Thus encouraged, the prisoner proves to be a model prisoner. He gives every indication of his reformation, and is taken at the expiry of the definite term before the board. He is hopeful of liberty and full of good resolutions, and the board announces that by reason of an earlier conviction, a fact well known to the judge who imposed the sentence, they will not allow him parole, and he must serve the indefinite term. I can imagine no situation more cruel and more likely to convert a man really desiring to reform into an enemy of society.
Indeterminate sentences had their origin in Michigan, and have been adopted in many places. Fundamentally reformatories are for up to one year and three hundred and sixty-four days definite, and by being indeterminate are made four years. The legality of the vvhole thing is questioned and the court of appeal makes criticisms on its usefulness.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: REPORTED INFECTION OF IMPORTED JAPANESE SHAVING BRUSHES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED INFECTION OF IMPORTED JAPANESE SHAVING BRUSHES
speechtext: I have a question to direct to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power). Has the government made any investigation into the report that certain imported Japanese goods said to be infected with anthrax germs were seized in Toronto this week by officials of the Ontario department of health working in cooperation with the Ontario provincial police? If so, will the government say what steps are being taken to protect the public from such dangers in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: REPORTED INFECTION OF IMPORTED JAPANESE SHAVING BRUSHES
speechtext:
My hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of his question. If the house will permit I might give a somewhat more extended answer than a merely categorical reply to the question.
On Saturday last the Department of Health received information from the head of the United States public health service, Surgeon-General Thomas Parran, to the effect that a case of anthrax which had been traced to a shaving brush had been discovered in North Dakota, and that it had resulted in a fatality. Immediately investigation was made by the United States authorities. The wholesale dis-

British Foreign Policy
tributing house which handled the brushes was questioned, and certain brushes seized and the hairs analyzed, with the result that a number were found to be contaminated with anthrax spores. Tracing the shipment still further to the distributing house in New York it was found that this house sold these brushes to a large number of variety stores throughout the United States and Canada. The surgeon-general of the United States advised the Canadian Department of Health that a number of these articles had been shipped to Canada, and gave the shipment numbers and the markings on the brushes. It was found that some had been distributed in the provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The health authorities of each of these provinces were advised as to these shipments and the stores to which they had been shipped. The medical health authorities in the other provinces were advised that shipments might have been made into those provinces. We have had replies from the health authorities of British Columbia, who have not as yet completed their investigations, and from Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, which found no brushes. The Ontario department of health found and seized a number of brushes which had been shipped into this country about two years ago. They are now proceeding to make an analysis, and the report of that analysis will not reach us until early next week. The Department of Health is in communication with the Department of National Revenue for the purpose of tracing any other such shipments to Canada and in order to inaugurate restrictions at the port of entry on similar shipments into Canada.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED CRITICISM BY VANCOUVER RESIDENT AND SUBSEQUENT ACTION BY MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
On Monday last the hon.
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) called attention to an item which appeared in The Nation, a periodical published in New York, to the effect that two members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had had an interview with a certain person who had been writing letters to Mr. Chamberlain criticizing British foreign policy in order to dissuade him from writing such letters, and that that gentleman answered that "just so long as postage stamps are available" he would keep on writing. My hon. friend wanted to know what the facts
were and whether such action is a part of government policy.
These letters were sent to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by Scotland Yard, in exactly the same way as Scotland Yard would investigate at the request of the Canadian police. The letters were not only abusive but scurrilous and libelous, contrary to the criminal code and in contravention of the postal regulations of Canada. In undemocratic countries anyone who wrote such letters as these would have been suppressed bymethods which are well known. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police merely tried to-convince that man that he should not write-such letters. If they erred in any way it wras on the side of leniency. The unfortunate part of it is that someone in a foreign country, just for the purpose of showing that the system is not good at the present time, should have written an item in disparagement of an administration of justice which bears comparison with the best existing anywhere.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: REPORTED CRITICISM BY VANCOUVER RESIDENT AND SUBSEQUENT ACTION BY MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
May I ask, is it usual for
Scotland Yard to communicate directly with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police? Should there not be a communication through the Secretary of State? Secondly, have we not courts? Why should there not have been a prosecution, instead of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police acting both as judge and policeman?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED CRITICISM BY VANCOUVER RESIDENT AND SUBSEQUENT ACTION BY MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Well,
Mr. Speaker, it is the practice not only here but in every civilized country that, when they are required to do so, police authorities may investigate for the police authorities of another country, especially in respect of illegal acts. The man who wrote that letter ought to be either in a lunatic asylum or in gaol. I do not think the hon. member is quite fair in criticizing the police for having given a warning to desist from writing those letters. Had the writer of the letters been prosecuted there would have been good souls who would have said that he was being persecuted for having written to Mr. Neville Chamberlain.
Members of the government are receiving letters of that kind. His Excellency the Governor General is receiving letters of that kind, and we are investigating in an effort to find out who are the crazy or guilty ones who are doing it, in order to try to prevent it. I am surprised to hear the hon. member criticize that course of action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like my first observation to be one of commendation of the hon. members who moved and seconded the address. Both performed in a most acceptable manner a difficult task, before a highly critical audience. Having lived in the constituency of Brandon for some twenty-five years, and having some knowledge of the political histoiy of that seat, I was particularly interested in the effort of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), who established himself as a worthy successor to that amiable and kindly gentleman, the late Mr. Beaubier, and to the long list of outstanding men who have represented that city in bygone years. It is significant that the hon. member who now holds the -seat is the first out-and-out Liberal to be *elected in Brandon since 1908, and that significant fact establishes the popular appeal the policies of this government have made to a seat which is both urban and rural. In addition, the hon. member came from Prince Edward Island, and forms part of the large group of maritimers who, having thrown in their lot with us, have made a substantial contribution to the building up and development of the last great west.
This is not the first occasion, Mr. Speaker, upon which the hon. member for Stormont {Mr. Chevrier) has captivated the house. I refer particularly to his address delivered in February, 1937, during the debate on the address in reply, upon which occasion he outlined the Liberal attitude towards capital and labour, and indicated a minimum which labour should receive. His address on that occasion will bear frequent perusal and I refer it to hon. members of the opposition who, while they have displayed an interest in jobs, have not shown any particular interest in that partnership of labour and capital which means security for employees. I forthwith exempt from that mild indictment the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling), who frequently has brought to the attention of the house the ideal conditions which prevail in the plant of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada, Limited, at Trail, British Columbia. By so doing he IMr. E, Lapointe.]
has given encouragement to industrialists throughout Canada to follow the excellent example of that company.
May I join with others in extending congratulations to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his selection as leader of the Conservative party and upon attaining a seat in the house. I was somewhat disturbed by a news dispatch of a couple of months ago which indicated that the great Conservative party had decided to abandon western Canada and the maritimes. It was with great relief I heard his declaration that there was no truth in that statement, that the great Conservative party was still an allCanadian party, and that in future it would function in western Canada. I am glad of that, and the hon. member both as leader of the Conservative party and personally may be assured of a cordial and warm welcome in the capital city of Saskatchewan.
May I extend my personal congratulations to the two new ministers who were honoured a few days ago. They bring to their jobs a long experience and a very high order of merit. The hon. minister without portfolio (Mr. MacKinnon) representing the constituency of Edmonton West, is a western man with an eastern background; the Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty) is an eastern man with a western background, having practised in western Canada for some nine years. They will therefore bring to the council chamber of the nation qualities designed to build an all-Canadian viewpoint.
I also join with hon. members who have expressed their pleasure upon the recovery of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) from his recent illness, a pleasure which was emphasized by the splendid reception accorded him when he entered the house on the opening day of the session. May I assure him that the sympathy extended to him by his innumerable friends throughout Saskatchewan was paralleled only by their relief and gratitude upon learning of his progress toward recovery, and by their expressed hope that he will soon be restored to that vigour which we in Saskatchewan know so well.
Apparently there was a meeting in Regina a few days ago, the subject matter of which was referred to by the hon. members for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) and Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), who attempted to magnify into something of national importance that which is really just a small and local matter. With that thought in mind the hon. member for Weyburn placed on Hansard a certain part of a newspaper dispatch. In order that we may recall the subject matter of the article, I shall repeat it:
Party men to decide.

The Address-Mr. McNiven
No jobs for others than Liberals, says Regina M.L.A.
A definite clamp has been placed upon the appointment of Regina residents to posts within the civil service that bars those whose political faith is other than Liberal, B. J. McDaniel, K.C., junior member-elect for Regina, told the meeting of the Liberal council at the Labour temple Tuesday night.
In future, said Mr. McDaniel, "no appointment will be deemed to be properly made unless it bears the initials of Mr. Hogarth (senior member-elect for Regina), Mr. McNiven (federal M.P. for Regina), or myself."
I am firm in the belief, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. McDaniel was either misreported or misunderstood, and in any event this forms an excellent example of what generally happens when a line, a sentence or a paragraph taken from a general discussion, is divorced from its context. A wrong impression of what was intended generally follows. I am confirmed in that belief because I know of no such arrangement as that described in the article in question. Further, in Saskatchewan there is what is known as a public service commission which looks after appointments, and hon. members know the extent to which the civil service commission has control over federal appointments. As an illustration of what I mean, within the last few weeks the provincial government appointed two police magistrates in the city of Regina. I was not consulted with regard to those appointments by any member of the Saskatchewan government, though I did make recommendations on behalf of individuals who asked me so to do.
During the course of that meeting an attempt was made to confine the discussion to the question of temporary appointments in the post office during the Christmas rush. When I was requested to assist the postmaster in securing extra help for the Christmas work I immediately got in touch with the various veterans' organizations, the Canadian legion, the war veterans' assistance commission, the army and navy veterans and the disabled war veterans, and asked them to furnish lists of those whom they could recommend. When the lists were furnished they were too lengthy for the employment that was available, and I asked the officers of these associations to select from their lists those whom they would recommend, having in mind the efficiency of the service and giving the preference to married men, particularly those with small children. This was done, and from those who interviewed me personally asking for employment a list of approximately 175 names was drawn up, which included those who had been recommended by the four service organizations. That list was forwarded to the postmaster in order that he might make the selection of
the help he required. Included among the individuals who came to see me was a returned soldier who had walked the streets of Regina for three months without a tooth in his mouth. He had served in France for two years, and I recommended him for employment so as to assist him in purchasing a set of teeth. I also promised him that further assistance would be forthcoming, from some source, in order to complete the purchase of a set of teeth.
No questions were asked as to political affiliations. The list was sent to the postmaster, and he made the selections therefrom as help was required. According to my information from the postmaster, 143 men were taken on during the Christmas rush. Of that number 31 were on what is described as the eligible list established by the civil service commission, who under the regulations were required to be given such employment as was available. Of the remainder 70 were returned soldiers, of whom 69 were married men. There were 42 civilians, of whom 33 had dependents. So I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this employment was divided on a fair, just and equitable basis, having regard to the efficiency of the service, and in accordance with the generally accepted principle of the greatest good to the greatest number.

the hon. member would have learned if he had referred to Mr. McDaniel's explanation of what occurred at the meeting. As an indication that this method met with general acceptance I have a telegram from F. J. Rowan, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian legion at Regina, addressed to myself, as follows:
Officers and members Canadian legion, Regina branch, express and desire to acknowledge publicly deepest appreciation your efforts in obtaining employment for ex-service men at post office during Christmas rush and on other occasions elsewhere.
The Address-Mr. McNiven

May I just mention that there have been other occasions when it was possible to provide employment in connection with work being done under the direction of the Department of Agriculture. Substantially the same method was followed on those occasions, with the approval of the Minister of Agriculture. Then I have another telegram from R. D. Lamont, secretary of the war veterans assistance commission at Regina:
No complaint from veterans' assistance commission re Christmas post office employees. Your cooperation entirely satisfactory.
I venture the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) could not conceive, much less execute, anything fairer than the manner in which the responsibility was discharged on this occasion. And, sir, that plan has been followed consistently since and including 1935, notwithstanding the fact that we in the city of Regina and the province of Saskatchewan had a harrowing experience with a coalition government made up largely of Conservatives but kept in office through the votes of friends and supporters of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group in this house. Between 1929 and 1934 that government dismissed hundreds of employees for no reason other than that they were Liberals. Men and women who had been employed by the government for twenty or twenty-five years were dismissed; and, sir, it is singular that Mr. McDaniel, who is the hero of this tempest in a teapot, was himself an employee of the provincial government in 1929.
In 1930 he was dismissed from office by that government notwithstanding the fact that he was a returned soldier, notwithstanding the fact that he had been decorated upon the field of battle and notwithstanding the fact that he had been seriously wounded and was able to progress down the streets of Regina only with the assistance of a cane. Members of the legislature friends and supporters of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group in this house by their votes kept that government in office from 1929 to 1934. But the hand of retribution fell heavily on them; for not a single supporter of that government was returned to office in 1934.

I believe that Mr. McDaniel has either been misreported or misunderstood, or the phrase has been taken from its context, with the damaging results that have been indicated.
I shall make only cursory reference to certain passages in the speech from the throne. Notwithstanding the continued efforts of its critics to weigh the speech from the throne by avoirdupois, or to measure it by yardage, by verbiage, by wordage and other methods, it becomes increasingly apparent that the speech from the throne is broad and comprehensive. When elaborated, as it was during the course of this debate by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), it is found to contain a broad and comprehensive program intended to carry to the homes of the people of this country the benefits of the policies of this government. So far as we in the west are concerned we welcome these trade treaties. We welcome the Canada-United States treaty in the same terms as it has been acclaimed in eastern Canada. The treaty of 1935 showed direct and positive benefits to those of us who reside in western Canada. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) pointed out yesterday, it did no specific harm to any existing business institution.	[DOT]
Some comment has been made doubting the significance of the international effects of the

The Address-Mr. McNiven
treaty. Never in the history of Canada or the United States have there been such friendly relations between the two countries as prevail at the present time, which relations have come about since the signing of that treaty in 1935. There is no doubt at all that the terms of the treaty of 1935 and the experience gained under it paved the way for the enlarged treaty of 1939. Once again doubts are being voiced as to the international effects to be obtained from this treaty. In this regard I should like to refer to the comment of Mr. Paul Van Zeeland, a former prime minister of Belgium, who was asked recently to make a report to the governments of France and the United Kingdom as to the possibility of obtaining a reduction in the number of quotas and the removal of other obstacles to international trade. Mr. Van Zeeland, in part, said:
-in the present state of affairs the negotiation of bilateral commercial agreements, based on the most favoured nation clause, remains one of the most efficacious methods for reducing tariff barriers.
And again, writing some ten months before the British-United States agreement was completed, he used this language:
No one would underestimate the effect which would be produced-either directly, in its reaction, on the two national economies concerned, or indirectly in its repercussion on the whole world, by the conclusion, in a spirit of international collaboration, of a commercial agreement covering a wide range between the two great Anglo-Saxon communities.
No matter what the critics of this agreement may say, the former prime minister of Belgium believes that it will have direct international effects with repercussions of benefit to the world. As an indication that tariffs are a disturbing element in the peace of the world, I should like to quote a short passage from the Fascist handbook which was issued on October 28, 1937. The following passage is to be found on page 88:
A prohibitive tariff policy was adopted by the United States; England first depreciated her currency and then closed her markets. The Ottawa agreements introduced differential tariffs throughout the British empire. Currency dumping vras practised on a large scale by Japan and other countries. Not content with tariffs, France introduced quotas and prohibitions, followed in this by most of the European countries, exchange regulations and blocked credits finally demoralized the markets, and paralyzed foreign trade.
For five long years from 1929 to 1934 Italy held out against the quotas and exchange control system. The Italian government participated in all efforts made by the league of nations and other international organizations in favour of freer trade, a policy which had the wholehearted support of her delegates, but all was in vain. The doctrines of exasperated "nationalism," economic "self-sufficiency" and manipulated currencies prevailed, and Italy had no choice but to resort to similar measures
in self-defence. But if the doctrine of economic "self-sufficiency" is to prevail, and if the settlement of international accounts by goods and services is ruled out, then the possession of adequate national resources is a question of life or death for a nation.
I should also like to cite this passage from the Nazi Primer at page 246:
Germany would in its present strained condition gladly and willingly buy from abroad the raw materials which we lack, if a sufficient possibility were given for doing so. Foreign countries, however, demand payment in foreign currency. The only way that we can obtain foreign money is by exporting German goods. In a senseless manner the countries with raw materials shut out German imports, isolate themselves in their great economic enclaves. Our exports have shrunk, therefore, in exactly the ratio that the revival of our country has increased our need for raw materials. For that reason the German economy in industry and handicrafts finds itself in very serious difficulties. If, therefore, German industry is to put all German workers back again, and to raise the production of goods to the point of doing awray with German poverty, extraordinary measures are necessary in order to obtain sufficient supplies of raw materials.
That is the attitude of the fascist and nazi governments, and it does seem to me that some move might be made by our government towards improving our trade relationships with these countries. I am told, for example, that there is a shortage of butter fats in Germany and Italy, while we have in storage some thirty to forty million pounds of butter. Could not a deal be made whereby the butter which Germany and Italy so much require could be exchanged for their products? Germany and Italy, in making such a deal, would be doing a good thing for their own countries, and at the same time the stress and strain on our economy would be relieved.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne to youth training. I shall make only a casual reference to that subject. Suffice it to say that in our province youth training has been a most interesting and productive experiment. In its first year of operation some nine thousand young men and women trained in the courses then provided, and some 566 took the courses in Regina. The courses are being continued and extended so that now instruction is given in subjects running all the way from beauty culture to aeroplane mechanics. A few days before I came down here I visited a home where a class was in progress for the training of domestic workers. They are making a splendid success of that undertaking, training girls for useful work in the future. Much has been said, and much may be said, about flaming youth, but that our young people are taking an interest in preparing themselves for the future is

The hon. member for Carleton, in his endeavour to establish that there W'as discord and disunity throughout Canada, referred to the province of Saskatchewan, and said:
I am not criticizing the government for the money that has been spent in that province-

For that I thank him.
-but writh all the money that was spent, even to win a provincial election, what do we find?
May I assure the hon. gentleman that if he had in mind federal money, there was no federal money spent in the province of Saskatchewan to win an election. What do we find?-he asked, and then proceeded to say:
They have raised the threat of secession-
And in order to establish that fact he quotes a resolution which reads as follows:
The United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, devoted a long debate to the subject at its annual convention and unanimously adopted a resolution instructing its board of directors "to assimilate and prepare authoritative material on the subject of setting up a western autonomous state within the British empire, governed by a single government elected democratically by the people."
Shortly after that resolution was passed, one of the leading newspapers of Saskatchewan, with a province-wdde circulation, provided through its columns for a vote on the question of secession and one or two kindred questions. Just to show you, Mr. Speaker, that secession is not an issue at all, is not even being considered in Saskatchewan, approximately only three thousand people made any response at all and gave their view's, and of those who did respond about one-half voted in favour of consideration of some such resolution as the hon. member quoted, while the rest wrere diametrically opposed to anything in the nature of secession. The fact that only three thousand people, out of a population of nearly one million, would pay any attention to the matter at all, is proof positive to me that there is nothing in the way of a threat involving secession from confederation. But seeing that agriculture, the bad crops and the distress in Saskatchewan have been referred to from time to time I thought it might be permissible, even at the risk of criticism for being narrow and parochial to address the rest of my remarks to conditions in that province.
Western Canada contains the finest expanse of good agricultural land to be found anywhere in the world, and the largest block intact, of that description, lies in Saskatchewan. In sixty-two years western Canada has produced 8,900,000,000 bushels of wheat valued at 10,200 million dollars; and in that same period it has exported 6,100 million bushels of wheat valued at 7,200 million dollars. In other words, in sixty-two years western Canada has brought into the country in the way of new wealth a sum equivalent to the entire debt of the whole of the dominion, federally, provincially, municipally and individually.

From 1918 to 1929 in our province alone we produced 4,150 million dollars of new wealth. For 1926, 1927 and 1928 our agricultural production was valued at $1,200,000,000 and in the year 1928 alone it amounted to nearly $500,000,000. And then the holocaust! From 1930 to 1935, a period of six years, production only totalled $817,000,000. The 1936 crop was reduced to 110,000,000 bushels, the 1937 crop was 37,000,000 bushels, and in 1938 our wheat crop approximated 140,000,000 bushels. These are astronomical figures, but conditions in the last eight years have exacted a terrific toll.
It may be asked, with that production why cannot you take care of yourselves? There are many reasons, prominent among them being the fact that certain laws, supply and demand and the currency question, have not been allowed to work out as they should have done; and western agriculture lias been the sufferer in every instance. Let me go back to the year 1917. In that year wheat sold at $3.05 a bushel on the Winnipeg grain exchange. The exchange was closed and a fixed price of $2.18 was made payable for the crops of 1916, 1917 and 1918, and that at a time when the United States farmer was selling his wheat at a price as high as $4.50 a bushel. The western farmer did not complain, but if you wish to ascertain the western farmers' contribution to the winning of the war, just multiply the production of each one of the prairie provinces by at least $1.50 or possibly $2 a bushel and you will get it. You will then know what the western farmers' contribution was to the winning of the war.
Wheat was the only commodity over which the government of the day took control, and notwithstanding that fixed price, the farmer had to pay war prices for everything he had to buy. During the deflationary period of 1930, 1931 and 1932 the Canadian dollar was tied to the United States dollar. I fully appreciate why that was done, but at the same time export commodities, principally wheat, had to meet competition with countries that had depreciated currencies, namely, the Argentine and Australia. At a time when the British pound was quoted at $3.70 it simply meant that the western agriculturist received less in terms of Canadian dollars than he would have got had the Canadian dollar been tied to the British pound. The hope of the western farmer lies in providing against wide fluctuations in price such as from $3 a bushel down to 38 cents, which was the prevailing price in 1932.
May I make one reference to the value of western farm lands as a matter of defence. Two years ago I heard Sir George Paish, one of the leading economists of the British empire, say that the war could not have been won, or in other words that the war would have been lost, had it not been for the bountiful crops of western Canada in 1915 and 1916 and the ability of the British government to transport those crops overseas. The most effective contribution that Canada can make to the defence of the empire and of our own country itself is in maintaining the wheat lands of western Canada and maintaining the population there on a reasonable standard of living.

May I at the outset congratulate the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), who has just made an excellent speech. It did seem to me, though, that it was a shame that so much of his time should have been taken up in explaining the rather questionable activities of one of his colleagues in Regina. It might be said of him, as has been said of others on other occasions, that he is blessed with one of the best friends a man was ever cursed with. Unfortunately, the " McDaniels " are not all located in western Canada or in Regina. I fear there are many in other part's of Canada and, if I may say so, the unjust patronage which is rampant in certain sections of the dominion is one of the greatest enemies of our democracy.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne upon the excellence of their speeches. I fancy they are becoming weary of congratulations; nevertheless the congratulations have been well deserved.
I was particularly interested in the remark of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven) with reference to the mover of the address in that he was a maritime province man. It has often occurred to me, as it must have to others throughout this dominion, to wonder just what other parts of Canada would have done had the maritime provinces not supplied them with their leading men in various activities of life.
I wish to congratulate the new Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty) upon his appointment to that very important office. It is a well deserved tribute to his ability, and I am satisfied that in the short time he will hold that office he will do credit to it. I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) upon his promo-
The Address-Mr. Brooks

tion. While he is not a maritimer I believe he did the next best thing; he went to the maritime provinces and took one of our fair daughters as his wife. I have no doubt that the inspiration which he received and the success which he has attained are due to the good advice he received from that source.
In my province of New Brunswick we have been thrilled, as the people all over Canada have been, by the prospective visit of Their Majesties the King and Queen. I am sure their visit to our dominion is an expression of their love of and loyalty to the people of this country, just as the great welcome they will receive will be an expression of the love and loyalty of the people of Canada for them. In my own constituency of Royal we expect to have the pleasure of a rather more extended visit than some other constituencies in Canada are to enjoy. King's county, in which I reside, is one of the few counties in which their majesties are to take a motor trip. Driving from Moncton to Sussex they will see the beautiful Kennebecasis valley, and on their trip from Fredericton to Saint John they will have the pleasure of seeing the beautiful Saint John river.
The speech from the throne made reference to the formal visit of the President of the United States to the Dominion of Canada. We in New Brunswick had many visits from Mr. Roosevelt before he became president. He spent many of his boyhood days on the beautiful little island of Campobello in the bay of Fundy, and doubtless the good feeling he entertains for this country and for the people of the British empire was more or less inspired by his contact with that part of Canada.
There is a criticism I should like to make with reference to visits of distinguished guests to our country, and it is this: that on too many occasions they are led to believe that Canada begins at Montreal and ends on the Pacific coast. Only last year a number of such visits were organized, supposed to be to eastern Canada. One party consisting of 200 Scottish school boys came out to see the eastern part of this country; their itinerary embraced Quebec, Montreal, the Laurentian mountains, Ottawa, Hamilton, Niagara Falls, London, Port Stanley, Toronto and Kingston, but did not include the maritime provinces. Another party of 200 under the auspices of the Overseas League-this by the way was the largest party organized by the Overseas League in the United Kingdom for travel in Canada, and represented one of the most important steps in furthering the chief aim of the league, namely, the cementing of friendly relations between the different parts of the 
British commonwealth of nations by the actual exchange of visits-this party visited Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto and Niagara Falls, and returned to Great Britain, although the tour also purported to cover the eastern provinces. A similar thing happened to the British parliamentarians who visited Canada recently; they commenced their visit at Quebec and ended it at Vancouver and Victoria. This is unfair to the three eastern provinces, and I hope that those who are responsible for such visits will see that this neglect is not continued.
The speech from the throne refers to the very important matter of defence. I am sure that all citizens of Canada to-day realize that defence is one of our most urgent necessities, and one of the biggest problems facing us. With world conditions what they are and have been for the past number of years, with nations seeming to be preparing to spring at one another's throats, and with conditions such as they have been in Ethiopia and Spain and China, it almost looks as if this old world were slithering back to the Middle Ages. If an emergency comes it will come quickly, so we must be prepared. I commend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) for the preparations he is making; I can only say that they are belated and not as extensive as they should be. In this morning's paper we see that a sum of $63,-
500,000	is to be provided for the defence of Canada, to be expended over a period of years. In the newspapers a short time ago we noticed that the Commonwealth of Australia also realizes that she must defend her territory against possible invasion. That dominion with only seven million people has voted some $250,000,000 to be expended over a period of three years. Australia is spending for defence something over $11 per person, while in our present estimate we are proposing to expend $5 per person.
I feel that we in eastern Canada have again been neglected as far as defence is concerned. The ports of Saint John and Halifax are without any adequate defence. We are told that the aeroplane is a great arm of defence. Other authorities tell us that the aeroplane is not the proper weapon for defence of cities and ports. Be that as it may, I am satisfied that at these two ports on the eastern coast we must have more antiaircraft guns, more artillery and coast defence. These I believe, as the minister told me last year, will take something like three years to provide.
As a maritimer I feel that we have another quarrel with the Minister of National Defence. I notice in this morning's paper that

The Address-Mr. Brooks
SI,800,000	is appropriated for Royal Canadian Air Force works in Nova Scotia. Last year I complained, and I complain again, that no appropriation has been made for military air fields in New Brunswick. We consider the port of Saint John just as necessary to the commercial life of this country, and of the maritime provinces in particular, as the port of Halifax; and it seems singular that there should be SI,800,000 spent in Nova Scotia, and five military air fields established in that province, and not one in New Brunswick. This item says:
More than $1,800,000 will be appropriated for the R.C.A.F. works in Nova Scotia. These embrace $919,000 for four hangars and other works at Dartmouth; $170,000 for runways at Yarmouth; $570,000 for runways at Sydney and $258,000 for magazines, quarters and runways at Truro.
If we are to defend the port of Saint John by air I claim there should be a military air field in the vicinity of that city. I also wish to give my approval to the formation of the defence purchasing board. It rather looks as if this is the direct result of the Davis report, and I would say it is all to the good for both Canada and the department. There is no member of this house, and I am sure there is no right thinking person in Canada, who does not feel that as far as profits are concerned there should be none from the various activities necessary to equip the militia of this country. I hope the activities of this board will be extended to include all the operations of the defence department, including both the permanent and the non-permanent militia.
Last year I called to the attention of the minister a matter which he admitted was a mess as far as his department was concerned. That was in connection with the building of the Venture by the Meteghan Shipbuilding Company in Nova Scotia, and I believe that matter has not been settled yet. The man who obtained that contract never would have been considered, I am sure, if there had been a board of this kind. In the first place the contractor was not capable of handling such a contract, and it is common knowledge that his men have not beep, paid, that the selection of the men for the work reeked with patronage and that labour was being exploited. Finally the Minister of Labour had to have an investigation into the activities of this company.	*
Now I come to a matter which is of very great importance to Saint John, the port of my own province, and also to Halifax. According to reports appearing in the newspapers of that part of the country, people are not satisfied with the explanation given
by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) here a few days ago. He quoted figures to show that there had been more wheat shipped from Canada in the five years prior to 1932 than in the five years following 1932. He did not say to what ports he was referring, nor did he give what is perhaps the chief explanation, that there was less wheat produced in Canada in the latter five years. According to my information, during the five years prior to 1932 we produced 2,056,244,000 bushels of wheat, while during the five years from 1932 to 1937 we produced only 1,241,304,000 bushels, or not much more than half as much. So it would not be logical to argue that during the five years in which we produced over two billion bushels of wheat there should not be more exported than during the period when we produced only a little over a billion bushels.
The minister also quoted from a report appearing in the Telegraph-Journal of January 10, under the heading, Grain Shipments Key to Port Problem, Workers Maintain. He was answering, as it were, the contention made by the heads of the longshoremen's association in Saint John. The president of that association is Leicester Wearing and the secretary is James Steen. These men are thoroughly informed in regard to everything concerning the port of Saint John, the shipping of grain and other commodities, rates and charges, and, in fact, all matters pertaining to the port. In an open letter regarding conditions in Saint John they have this to say:
That we are of the opinion that when the Anglo-American trade pact was signed, Canada was sadly neglected. The fact that British millers, within a week after pact was signed, placed an order for half a million tons of wheat with American shippers, coupled with the knowledge that in the last few days steamers have left our port to go to Baltimore to load grain, is sufficient proof for the members we represent to make this statement.
They also go on to say that the day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) made the statement that the Anglo-American trade pact was one of the greatest achievements of the Canadian year, grain shipments through Saint John to steamers amounted to S74.473 bushels as against 5,024,716 bushels on the same day the previous year; while on track and in elevator there were 337,437 bushels as compared with 2,418,763 on the same day in the previous year. Speaking of trade going to the American ports they say:
We do not expect the trade conditions in this port to show much improvement in the near future; steamers are leaving here with only part cargoes, some calling at American ports to complete loading. . . .

Mr. Brooks

During December the steamer Brant County came to Saint John, discharged a few hundred tons of freight and went to Baltimore to load a full cargo of grain.
The S.S. Cape Lena came here with 160,000 bushels of wheat loaded at Baltimore.
There is talk of the S.S. Melmore Head, now in port, discharging coal, going to Baltimore for grain.

. . . never in the experience of the writer (nineteen years at this work) has work been so poor as this year has proven to be; and it was forecast on December 8, when this local took this matter, along with other points in dispute, up with Hon. Mr. Howe. . . .
Let me assure you that conditions here are terrible in so far as port business is concerned, and our members are not earning sufficient to keep their families while in previous years, at this time, they would be quite comfortable.
Irregardless of what Messrs. Howe, Euler, Michaud and Gardiner state in their remarks during sessions, the fact that steamers are coming here, discharging a few hundred tons of cargo and sailing to American ports to pick up Canadian grain, is convincing enough proof that there is some advantage over our port held by United States ports, and we are of the opinion that the preference abolishment, coupled with bonuses to American wheat exporters by U.S. government and railroad freight charges and elevation charges reduced, are the causes.

Steps should be taken to see that Canadian ports do not suffer as a result of competition from ports outside the dominion boundaries. If Canada is to gain the full benefits possible from the grain trade, which is heavily subsidized with federal funds to which all parts of Canada contribute, then no circumstance should be disregarded which will guide the flow of that trade over Canadian transportation

systems and through Canadian ports. The case presented to Ottawa by the Saint John Board of Trade should have the weight of Canadian public opinion behind it, and it should receive from the Ottawa authorities the attention which its national importance demands.

I am sure there are hon. members who will agree with me when I say that the loss of our salt fish market in the West Indies has been due to that treaty. Margaret Bondfield, a former minister of labour in the British government. She made a visit to Canada and the United States to study labour conditions, and speaking with reference to the youth in the United States she said:
Young men are made to feel that their country is looking after them.
Referring to Canada she had this to say:
It appears that no one takes the slightest responsibility for the Canadian youth once he is unemployed.
That is a terrible indictment of this government. It is a terrible indictment of our country.
In closing I have just a word or two to say about economic appeasement. I wonder why in a democratic country there should be talk of the necessity of economic appeasement in order to defend democratic institutions. What are the great democratic countries of the world? They are France, England and the United States. Is it not logical and reasonable to expect that these three nations should stand together both for their own defence and for the defence of democracy? We in Canada are very proud of France and England. During the great war these two nations fought shoulder to shoulder, and I believe they were fighting the battles of democracy. They are still standing shoulder to shoulder, but it is just as much in the interests of the United States that democracy should survive in this world as it is in the interests of the British empire or in the interests of France. Why then should we talk of economic appeasement?
The Prime Minister prates of health and peace and sweet content being the rightful heritage of all. Why should the longshoreman and the workingman in the city of Saint John, for example, be sacrificed for the economic appeasement of the longshoreman and workingman in Baltimore or some other
port of the United States? Why should the primary producers and our workers in the factories of this country be sacrificed for the economic appeasement of workers elsewhere? I do not believe that the American people require it; I do not believe they want it. I believe they are willing and anxious to stand shoulder to shoulder with the British empire and France in the defence of that democracy which we all love. In this recent treaty I fear that Canada has again paid too high a price, and that the treaty is out of balance, as far as lasting benefits to Canada are concerned.

But at this time I intend to confine my attention to those references in the speech from the throne which deal with national defence and the proposed defence purchasing board. I am aware that these matters will be discussed in more detail later; nevertheless, in view of certain recent disquiet-rg disclosures. 1 believe the government should at the earliest possible date give more adequate assurances that conditions repugnant to the public interest will be rectified.
In the forecast of the legislative program set forth in the speech from the throne, priority is given to the proposal to increase substantially appropriations for national defence and for the establishment of a defence purchasing board. At this stage I shall not attempt to discuss whether such increased appropriations are justified, but I express the hope that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) will take the house fully into his confidence as to the policies to be pursued and as to the manner in which these huge sums will be applied. It is important that the government, before embarking on such policies, should give more definite assurances than have heretofore been given that Canada will receive full value in defence measures for every dollar spent on defence. Increased defence appropriations will place additional burdens on the Canadian taxpayer and will demand of the Canadian people further sacrifices. Clearly we have reached the point where increased expenditure for this purpose will retard the promotion and development of necessary social services. Before launching a still greater spending program to provide armaments for Canada, this country has a right to expect the closest and most rigorous scrutiny of the spending method? of
The Address-Mr. MacNeil

those to whom t he administration of those vast sums is entrusted. The competency of these men is now a matter of grave doubt.
The minister has stated publicly on more than one occasion that because of the limitations of the appropriations made by parliament he could not make satisfactory progress in providing for the defence of Canada. It is now evident that something more than huge appropriations are needed to guarantee us defence against external dangers. In the period between 1918 and 1937 something in the vicinity of three hundred million dollars was expended in defence. Yet the minister in 1937 rose in his place and said that defence had been so neglected that Canada was without any means of defence. Apparently the trifling sum of approximately three hundred million dollars entrusted to the general staff had gone with the wind.
In the last two years an additional seventy million dollars has been made available to the defence department. Apparently with regard to coastal defence the results achieved have been negligible. No one can understand where the money has gone. The sums voted by parliament in the last three years, approximately ninety million dollars, should have made evident some effective measures of coastal defence. Must we conclude that the clue to the mystery is to be found in the recent judicial inquiry into the Bren machine gun contract? One contract out of many was submitted to a searching inquiry, and the most amazing circumstances have been disclosed. We knew that the Department of National Defence was becoming one of the biggest spending departments of the government. We now have good cause to regard it as the most wasteful and inefficient. We have good cause to ask if the additional millions requested from parliament are actually for the defence of Canada or for the defence of the profits of the privileged ring of armament manufacturers. We now discover that department officials have shown the most arrogant disregard of policies enunciated in parliament and accepted by parliament in good faith. It now rests with parliament to determine whether there has been a gross betrayal of public trust.
During the last session members of this group endeavoured to obtain from the Minister of National Defence more definite information regarding the conditions under which the Bren machine gun contract had been negotiated and executed. We got from the minister in this regard little more than the most eloquent assurance that it was the best of all possible contracts for the Dominion of Canada. It is a matter of regret that the
(Mr MarNpil.1
minister did not discuss the matter with greater frankness and that it required a judicial inquiry to unearth facts which should have been in the possession of the house when the matter was under consideration. The minister can no longer boast that it is one of the finest contracts ever made on behalf of Canada. I venture to predict that it will prove to be one of the most humiliating episodes in his public career.
It was claimed in press releases at the time the commissioner's report was tabled that the department had received complete exoneration. Nothing could be further from the truth. No one was exonerated except in the matter of personal graft and corruption, which was never in question. The very fact that the commissioner found it necessary to recommend an entirely new method of awarding contracts of this kind is by implication a condemnation of the method followed in this instance. If it had been shown that the method of placing government contracts followed in this instance had been entirely satisfactory, the commissioner would have said so. Instead he recommends a drastic change in the whole system. The government now finds it necessary to act on this recommendation. The methods which we questioned last year, and which were then defended by the government, must now be discarded because the public interests were then inadequately safeguarded. The condemnation of departmental administration is indirect, nevertheless so plain that he who runs may read.
In an editorial the Winnipeg Tribune aptly said that the commission might be described as having done a very neat job of washing its hands and holding its nose alternately. It also said that Mr. Justice Davis had parked that squawling brat, the Bren gun contract, right back on the dominion government's doorstep where it belongs. That exactly describes the situation in language which is easily understood. The commissioner places on record certain facts with regard to which he reports there was no dispute. He states:
It will be for those charged with the responsibility of dealing with the facts, i.e., the government and parliament, to examine and study them and to take such action, if any, as they may sec fit.
Further than this, the commissioner places certain issues squarely before parliament. Parliament is asked to judge on the facts in evidence, as to-
(1)	Whether Bren guns should be produced by the government in publicly-owned fac-

tories or through private manufacture (page 10 of the report).
(2)	Whether the conduct of the individuals *concerned was above question (page 35).
(3)	Whether adequate reasons existed for the failure of the interdepartmental committee to report back to the government when the system of supervision of contracts broke down (page 41).
(4)	Whether the procedure followed in negotiating this contract protected the public interest (page 49).
(5)	Whether proper steps were taken to ensure proper discharge of the responsibility assumed in the selection of a favoured contractor (page 50).
I contend that these issues should be dealt with by parliament before we approve further appropriations to be administered by those whose administrative competency is now a matter of grave doubt.
From time to time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) have given assurances in this chamber as to the policies that would be pursued in placing armament contracts. I submit that the facts disclosed in the commissioner's report indicate that in many important respects no attempt was made to give effect to these policies in administration. As a matter of fact, it is shown by the evidence that the intentions of the government as declared in the house and accepted in good faith were evaded and even thwarted by those responsible for the negotiations leading up to the execution of this contract. This administration is on record as favouring the principle of public ownership as applied to the manufacture of armaments, particularly during peace time. When on the witness stand, the Minister of National Defence was most emphatic in his declaration on this point. The evidence shows that senior officers with responsible positions on the defence council had advocated the establishment by the government of a plant capable of meeting the requirements of the Canadian forces in respect to the Bren gun. These officers pointed to the unsatisfactory results which had followed the placement of similar orders in privately-owned factories in other dominions. The minutes of the defence council as recorded in the evidence make it quite clear that in 1936 there was a considerable weight of technical opinion on the side of public ownership. The original agreement between the British government and the patentee stipulated that manufacture in the dominions should be in a factory operated by the government in question. Even while Major Hahn was in England negotiating for
his contract, the chief of general staff argued in a memorandum made in October, 1936, for the establishment of a government-operated rifle and gun plant. If manufacturing in government plants was ever seriously contemplated, why was a favoured contractor commissioned to secure secret information in England for his own purposes when at that time an officer of the Department of National Defence had the necessary technical information?
The reason given by the minister, when on the stand, for his non-adherence to the principle of public ownership was the limitations of appropriations made by parliament. He described these appropriations as meagre and stated that it was impossible even to make a start towards the establishment of government-operated plants. When the Bren gun was under consideration, he stated that he had been provided with an estimate showing that from 830,000,000 to 835.000,000 would be required to proceed with such a scheme. Actually, when this estimate was mentioned in the minutes of the defence council, it referred to the creation of a complete group of government manufacturing establishments on a scale that would meet all the requirements of the Canadian forces.
The commissioner was in doubt upon this point, for at page 11 of the report he says:
But the testimony given before the commission established that only 00,000 square feet of space was necessary for the purpose of production of the 7,000 Bren guns for Canada as well as 5,000 guns for the War Office and that an entirely new building (apart from land) would cost approximately $120,000. In proposal "B" of Major Hahn (Exhibit 11) of December 29, 1936, the building was shown at an estimated cost of $104,196.40.
This testimony should be considered in conjunction with the terms of the contract which placed government equipment at Valcartier and Quebec at the disposal of the John Inglis Company and made provision for a substantial reimbursement on the purchase of additional equipment required. No real attempt was made to explore the possibilities of public manufacture. It does not require an expert accountant to show that a government-owned plant might have been established, as originally stipulated by the British government, at a cost within the bounds of the appropriations made by parliament.
Furthermore, apparently no attempt was made to examine the possibilities of manufacture in plants already under government control. It was reported to the house last session that a complete survey had been made of such plants, and we know there are such
The Address-Mr. MacNeil

For some time the British government insisted upon its desire to deal with the Canadian government and not directly with a Canadian manufacturer. The report makes it clear that from the earliest stage of the discussions and negotiations it was the aim of the department to secure a complementary order from the War Office for Hahn's firm. Subsequently Colonel Orde, judge-advocate-general, assisted in drafting the contract between the British authorities and the John Inglis Company. The commissioner states 'That pressure from Canada upon the War Office during the period was continuous is in my view the proper inference from the facts directly proved in evidence." Contrary to the statement made by the minister in the house last session, it was this pressure for a full year from the Department of National Defence which secured a profitable contract from the British government for the John Inglis Company. I refer to the minister's statement which appears at page 3555 of Hansard for June 3, 193S.
The Prime Minister also assured the house that all such contracts would be reviewed by the interdepartmental committee. The commissioner in his report points to the breakdown of this system and to the failure of the committee to report back to the government, The chairman of this committee is the deputy minister of the Department of National Defence. The committee wanted to get price comparisons from other competent companies. They kept urging some method of competitive bidding. The chairman indicated that he had then an understanding that the British authorities would not deal with any other firm. Later, in February, 193S. he intimated to the committee that the British government had picked the John Inglis Company. When the committee suggested that a cablegram be sent to the British War Office asking, "Will you or will you not deal with a selected list of companies?" the deputy minister is reported as feeling very strongly about the matter and practically insisting that they must not take such action. The committee was forced to accept the deputy minister's word that the British government would deal with no other company than the John Inglis Company.
This becomes a serious matter when the proceedings of the interdepartmental committee are viewed in the light of the negotiations conducted with the British government from 1936 and the pressure actually exercised to persuade the British government to place an order with one particular company. The minister accepts full responsibility for the

actions of the officers of his department. I look to him to explain whether or not the committee was shamefully deceived and misled as to the true facts in the case.
The truth about the situation must be plain to every hon. member who reads the report. It was one of the rankest and most barefaced political patronage deals ever foisted upon a long-suffering public. When political patronage is admitted at the back-door, all businesslike and patriotic considerations are thrown out of the window. This becomes especially serious when patronage is extended to armament contracts. Patronage becomes the most convenient cloak for our profiteers to cash in on the profits of the next war. The report of the commissioner contains one clear-cut illustration of how patronage operates to block ordinary, clean, honest, businesslike methods. On August 24, 1936, the hon. member for Trinity wrote to the Prime Minister stating that a group of friends in Toronto were fully equipped to manufacture munitions. On October 25, 1936, the deputy minister, following several conversations, wrote to the Department of External Affairs asking that Major Hahn be sponsored in the British War Office by the high commissioner. He described Major Hahn as representing- and I quote:
-a reliable group, which controls certain manufacturing plants, capable of manufacturing armament and munitions-
He did not wait until he had received a report on the plant from the officers of his department, but subsequently he did receive a report which reads in part as follows, and I am quoting from page 22 of the commissioner's report:
This plant is primarily equipped for the manufacture of boilers, turbines and the working of heavy plate generally. _ All equipment is in reasonably good condition, considering the length of time it has been in use.
The machinery at present in this factory with few exceptions is unsuited for the manufacture of aircraft, but it might be used for the manufacture of tanks or shells . . *_
This factory is at present inoperative and has not been in operation since April, 1936, There is no design staff at present employed and the total number of workmen now employed consists of three men as factory maintenance staff.
Another officer reported:
This firm is equipped to do heavy engineering work, boilers, etc. The shops would require to be stripped of their equipment to be suitable for aircraft construction. The shops are more suitable for shells, gun carriages, etc., than for aircraft or aircraft engines.
Thus it appears that both the communication of the hon. member for Trinity and the communication of the deputy minister were grossly inaccurate.

During the argument by counsel special reference was made to that inaccuracy and to the responsibility of the hon. member in that regard. There is no evidence to show that this information was communicated to the British War Office. Apparently the British authorities were allowed, during the negotiations which followed, to proceed on the assumption established in the letter of the deputy minister. The minister gave evidence on the stand that he did not know the personnel of the group behind Major Hahn, and did not know what previous experience they had in the manufacture of precision steel; he stated that he was completely in the dark on these matters. The deputy minister also swore that he did not know who were included in this "reliable group." According to the report, not until May, 1937, were any inquiries made as to the financial standing of Major Hahn, when a banker's reference was obtained. Why were ordinary business precautions so grossly neglected, if there was not the determination to place this contract to the advantage of political friends?
The report confirms statements I have made on previous occasions with regard to the inefficiency of the Department of National Defence. There is evidently a lamentable lack of coordination between the administrative and technical branches. If these huge expenditures are to provide a party "pork-barrel," we shall get little in the way of actual defence. I suggest that hon. members read the volume of appendices issued with the first volume of the official war history and refresh their memories as to the humiliating experiences in connection with war purchases during 1914-1918. It would be well to remember now, in the light of these disclosures, the Ross rifle, the Oliver equipment, the Bain wagon, the motor equipment and spare parts, and so on. Read the exchange of cablegrams between the Canadian authorities and the British War Office. When boots of Canadian manufacture were condemned by
the British higher command, the Canadian authorities, to satisfy profiteering interests in Canada, ordered thousands of overshoes which were never used and which never could have been used by men in the front line. For similar reasons they let contracts to remodel the Oliver equipment, all of which was later dumped somewhere, and so on ad nauseam. A number of painful inquiries were held by committees of this house, during which the most scandalous evidence was unearthed. Because of these things, the lives of our troops were exposed to additional and needless risk in the most callous manner.
There can no longer be any doubt but that these misdeeds found their root in political patronage. Much was forgiven because of the emergencies of war time. There can be no such excuse for similar practices now which may lead to results quite as iniquitous during crises of the future. The mere appointment of a defence purchasing board does not meet the situation. The responsibility lies upon the government to deal severely with those who have been playing political "ducks and drakes" with defence appropriations. Defence purchasing must be freed entirely from political patronage.
Because of this report, which is not at all reassuring but definitely alarming, I urge that an inquiry be made by this house or by a committee of this house into the facts cited by the commissioner, to which I have referred, together with the related evidence. I also urge the drastic reorganization of the Department of National Defence, to accomplish greater efficiency and coordination. Further. I urge the nationalization of armament manufacture.

Mr. Speaker, my first words will be an expression of the joy felt throughout Canada, and already voiced by many hon. members, at the coming visit of our king and queen. The joyous anticipation felt by the people of Canada has been properly expressed in the speech from the throne. I think I can add that it is felt with particular keenness in the province of Quebec. Canada's recent history reveals numerous reasons why we, a minority, should show our attachment to the British crown. Especially since the enactment of the statute of Westminster, we can say: the King of Canada. We sincerely hope, particularly we of the province of Quebec, that their majesties' visit to Canada will be a most pleasant one. We are sure that throughout the country they will find, wherever they go, an atmosphere of cordiality and of attachment to the British crown.
The Address-Mr. Tremblay

The speech from the throne also makes reference to the visit which the president of the neighbouring republic paid to Canada last summer. We are particularly glad of it. Indeed, it is comforting to note, in these times of universal distrust, the friendly relations existing between Canada and the United States and which are an example to the world. All will admit, I venture to say, that through his personality and intellectual outlook the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) enjoys valuable friendships abroad, which have been of distinct benefit to us.
Not very long ago an Ottawa newspaper paid the following tribute to the Prime Minister. I quote from the Ottawa Evening Citizen of February 15th, 1937:
The spirit of Canada, the spirit of friendly cooperation, readiness to meet the other man half-way as the most hopeful way to make an enduring agreement, is reflected in every substantial achievement of the Prime Minister's long political career.
We can sincerely thank Providence that in these times of universal stress the present Prime Minister is directing the affairs of the country.
(Text) May I now offer my congratulations to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his election to the leadership of the party and subsequently to the house. He seems to be a very sympathetic gentleman, and all hon. members are pleased to welcome him. For many years he has been a leading figure in Canadian politics, and iwe Liberals were particularly gratified that our party did not oppose his election. Though I do not by any means wish to be disagreeable, may I add that having carefully listened to and read his speech on the address and having read and listened to the reply of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), our sense of security as Liberals is such that I am wondering whether the beau geste of the Prime Minister at the time of the London by-election was altogether disinterested.
May I extend my congratulations also to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) upon his able speech. He has good reason to be proud of his success in Brandon, and we are glad to welcome him among us.
(Translation) I also wish to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier). The legitimate feeling of pride which his success in this chamber has caused to us of French origin can easily be understood. He has revealed himself a brilliant politician and indefatigable worker, with an intelligent interest in all the difficult problems which confront the legislative bodies of the country. I trust his constituents will keep him a long time in the House of Commons, so that he may

fruitfully continue an already promising career.
The speech from the throne refers to present developments throughout the world, which are of grave concern not only to those charged with the administration of public affairs, but to the entire country, nay to all the countries of the world. Every day we anxiously open the papers to find out the latest developments in the international situation. Last September we all breathed a sigh of relief when, thanks to the intervention of the Prime Minister of England, Mr. Chamberlain, war was avoided at the last moment. Those of my generation especially, who vividly recall the horrors of the last war, rendered thanks to Providence that the intervention of the great English statesman had succeeded, for a time at least-for ever-in ensuring universal peace. I suggest that the leader of this country was largely responsible for that result. From nearly every quarter attempts were made to obtain from the right hon. the prime minister, or from the government, statements that would have committed Canada to one stand or another, but with his well known caution our leader was more than a match for those who wished to extort from him an ill-timed statement.
As stated in the paper I have just quoted, the right hon. the prime minister is a true Canadian, and I believe it is high time . that his Canadianism should be shared by other eminent public men who seem to have much more concern for the interests of the empire than for those of Canada. A few days ago, I was reading lectures and speeches delivered all over the country by the erstwhile leader of the Conservative party during his farewell trip. He is a former prime minister and the predecessor of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). He always gives the impression of having at heart the interests of the empire to the extent, I am afraid, of forgetting that the duty of a Canadian is, above all, to promote the interests of Canada. We have just one country: Canada. It is all very well to watch over the safety of the empire, but it is more legitimate and patriotic to look after the security of Canada.
I should like to read an article from the January 25th issue of the Liberal party's organ in Quebec, which I am sure reflects the opinion of the majority of my compatriots from Quebec. In an editorial entitled "His last will", Le Soleil, of Quebec city, had this to say:
To look after the safety of the empire, such is the ideal which Eight Honourable R. B. Bennett propounds to the young people of Canada, at a time when he is leaving this country to enjoy in England the consideration he has earned through his loyal services. The former

Tory leader is thus at variance with his political platform of 1930, which he used to sum up in two words: "Canada first." Moreover, in that farewell speech the words and the actions of the speaker are not in harmony.
