Here is what the hon. the leader of the opposition said:
If some of the right honourable gentlemen from the province of Quebec had not been so assiduous, in years gone by, in preaching to the people of that province the doctrine that this party was the militaristic party because we believed in a certain amount of defence about half of what we have to-day-if they had
not been so assiduous in building up prejudice___
they would not to-day find it so difficult to remove the prejudice which they built up in regard to defence.
Mr. Speaker, anyone who asserts that we, from the province of Quebec, are against defence is saying something that is absolutely unfounded. Nothing shows that such is the case. We have our own opinions and freedom to express them is the very essence of liberalism. A few of my hon. fellow-members have done so. By-elections have since been held in the province of Quebec and the armaments question has been discussed before the electors, and everywhere we have gained signal victories. To the hon. leader of the opposition who suggests that some of our leaders have built up prejudice in the 71492-23
province of Quebec, I will say that his statement is unfounded and unwarranted. But I remember quite well that some twenty years ago, the hon. the leader of the opposition was in sympathy with a government which succeeded in raising prejudice against the province of Quebec in all the other provinces of the dominion. We, from Quebec, do not claim that Canada should have no defence or armaments; on the contrary, but Canada is our only fatherland. We are neither French nor English, we are Canadians, and our only fatherland is Canada. When we are requested to vote for an increase in the estimates of the Department of National Defence for the protection of Canada and the defence of our territory, I say that Quebec is willing to support that, but we do not want to share any longer in foreign ventures; that is all we have said and that is the feeling of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, unemployment of course is a matter of concern for all governments. This government refers to it in the speech from the throne. Last year, it was my privilege in this house, to say a few words about the elimination of abuses in the organization set up for the relief of unemployment through projects initiated by the provincial authorities of Quebec or carried out by them in cooperation with the dominion government. I mentioned cases where the Quebec government showed discrimination against destitute people solely because they did not share their political opinions. It is a well known fact that the government of the province of Quebec refuses to cooperate with the dominion government, Last session I asked the government this question:	Is a responsible
government justified in asking the House of Commons to vote millions of dollars of the tax-payer's money to be spent by another government which has so often showed bad faith and from which no cooperation can be expected? Subsequent events force me to repeat this question and to ask if such a condition should continue.
Last year I had to inform the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) that I had repeatedly asked the administrators of the youth training plan in the province of Quebec, but always in vain, to give to some of my electors an opportunity of taking advantage of the plan. I am glad to acknowledge to-day that my recommendations have had at least partial effect, for I have since succeeded in my attempts on behalf of a certain number of unemployed young men residing in my constituency. It seems to me, however, that the application of the scheme could be extended somewhat. There are, for instance.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay

young men who would have liked to take courses at the Quebec technical school. I recommended some of them, but I was told that they could not be admitted this year under the youth training plan.
Youth is such an important factor in any nation that we ought to be more generous with regard to that part of our population. Our contribution to that plan should be larger in order to give young men and women, who have reached or will soon reach the age of earning their livelihood a chance to take advantage of the present depression to learn a trade that will enable them to serve the community at some future time.
The sons of our farmers cannot easily avail themselves of the opportunity offered by the youth training plan. May I suggest that extension courses in agriculture should be given more extensively? During the winter months, young people in the rural districts have practically nothing to do. If agricultural experts could visit the different parishes in order to give such extension courses, young people could improve their knowledge of agricultural sciences and prepare themselves to make a more useful contribution to the development of agriculture. Such an expenditure would prove to be a good investment. As I represent an almost exclusively rural district and am acquainted with the facts, I am satisfied that legislative bodies would do well to give more attention to the youth of our rural communities. I would therefore ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) to take such steps as may be necessary, under the federal-provincial agreement, to call the attention of the youth training committee to my suggestion.
Does the government propose entirely to assume the cost of old age pensions as some people have suggested? I cannot say. But let me urge upon the government, if provincial governments are to retain the administration of the act, the necessity of at least appointing federal inspectors to see that those who are entitled to it get a pension and to avoid any favouritism in that respect. In the province of Quebec, there is cause to complain of the shameful partiality shown by the provincial government. Consequently, the federal government would be well advised to ensure an equitable distribution of pensions.
During the Christmas holidays, I read a circular letter addressed to all those in receipt of government pensions by the Union Nationale member for the county of Dorchester. In that letter, he emphasized his solicitude in their behalf, and all the trouble he had taken in order to secure old age pensions for them. Mr. Begin added that,

so long as he is the representative of their electoral district, those poor old people could feel assured of their economic security, without mentioning that 75 per cent of their pension is paid by the federal government. I want to call the attention of the government to that fact, which shows that all possible means are used in the province of Quebec for political propaganda.
I desire to join with hon. members who have congratulated the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) for his recent statement in Montreal. 1 fully endorse the words not only of the minister but also of my fellow members, and especially of the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). I sincerely congratulate him for his speech in this chamber. He accurately expressed the sentiment of my compatriots of the province of Quebec. I heartily join with my desk-mate, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle) in congratulating the Secretary of State for his statement. We have nothing against any minority, but we are opposed to all immigration. We should solve our own problems instead of aggravating them and creating new difficulties. After we have found a job for every unemployed man in Canada, we will be in a position to cast a sympathetic eye on other nations of the world labouring under hardships. Until then, let us devote all our energies to the solution of our own problems.
In conclusion, sir, I again make this appeal to my fellow members and all Canadians: By all means, during the difficult days in which we live, let us act and think as Canadians. The affairs of our own country must engage all our attention. Let us silence those who create prejudices and try to set one class of society against the other in order to gain some personal benefit. United, we will be able to do something for Canada. Let us think a little more of Canada, our country, than the British empire.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commencing my remarks on the speech from the throne I should like to add a word of praise for the speeches of the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply. I thought the hon. member for Brandon spoke excellently and I have no doubt he was aided considerably by the odd timely nod and smile of your honour, which has meant so much to all of

The Address-Mr. Green
us new members in this parliament. Of course the hon. member for Stormont also spoke well; we all knew he would do so. Although one of our youngest members, he is one of our ablest and at the same time one of our most modest, and I have always believed that he is destined to render great service to Canada. I wish I could say as much for the government.
To-night, however, I aim to be entirely constructive in my criticism of the government, and I intend to offer them sincerely certain suggestions which I know will be accepted in the spirit in which they are given, I do this particularly because in these days, as we all know, there are literally thousands upon thousands of good Canadians who are unhappy and unsettled and whose lives could be greatly brightened if this government will only act at this session.
As the basis for my suggestions may I say that, looking back, I am convinced that from the start, from the year 1935, this government have made one great mistake. Of course, there have been many minor mistakes, but they have made one great mistake, and judging by the speech from the throne, and particularly by the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) delivered yesterday, they plan to persist in that same mistake, which is, in expecting too much from our export trade instead of placing equal importance upon improving directly the living conditions of the Canadian people.
Coming from the great Pacific port of Vancouver, one of the gateways of British Columbia, which is an export province, I realize to the full the importance of developing our overseas markets. But side by side with the development of those markets there should have gone policies for the improving of conditions within Canada. Take, for example, the 1935 trade agreement with the United States. That obviously did not solve our internal problems, and the new Canada-United States trade agreement, with the concessions made by Canada in respect of the United Kingdom agreement, will not solve these problems. They may help a bit; though I am afraid they will not, I hope they do. But no one in British Columbia, or at least no considerable body of people in that province, expects them to create many jobs. The people there fear that the agreements will wipe out present jobs. In fact the general reaction is the negative one, "Oh, well, they might have been worse."
But now that these trade arrangements are concluded, I urge the government to give its undivided attention to conditions within Canada, and particularly to the problem of what is to be done about Canadians on relief or on aid of one type or another, ranging in number from approximately three-
71492-23J
quarters of a million to a million as the seasons change, and that after we have been in a depression for eight or nine years. The government should also face the problem of what is to be done about those other Canadians, numbering no one knows how many thousands, who are living from day to day on the verge of relief, not actually on relief but very near it, in fear of what the morrow may bring forth. Both these groups are without security for future happiness and without much incentive to be enthusiastic over Canada or over Canadian institutions.
The speech from the throne offers these two groups very little more than the same old soothing syrup of'public works. We all admit that public works are not a solution; they are merely a stop gap; and yet that is what we are offered in the speech from the throne. For the permanent solution of the problem we have a promise. Promises are great things, and we have the promise that after the Rowell commission reports there is going to be a national conference at which, I quote from the speech from the throne:
. . . among the important subjects to be dealt with will be the problem of unemployment and social services generally.
In other words, this government is marking time on this issue of relief and security, continuing the great mistake that has been made by Canadian governments since the depression began, of treating unemployment as an emergency, treating it as something local and temporary, instead of what it is, a great national issue.
I suggest that at this 1939 session the government, while it still has the chance, take the first step toward providing unemployment insurance by passing an act authorizing the dominion to pay, to those provinces which set up a satisfactory unemployment insurance scheme, either the whole or part of the cost. This was the way in which Canadians got old age pensions. I would refer hon. members to section 3 of the Old Age Pensions Act, which tells the story. It reads.
The governor in council may make an agreement with the lieutenant-governor in council of any province for the payment to such province quarterly of an amount equal to seventy-five per cent of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions-
Then I stress these words:
-pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions specified in this act-
That is, the federal act.
-and the regulations made hereunder.
No doubt it would be more workable and less expensive to have unemployment insur-
The Address-Mr. Green

ance provided for under dominion law exclusively, but it seems obvious that the provinces will not agree that the dominion should have the necessary power. For example, I would refer the house to the speech from the throne in 1938, particularly to that portion dealing with unemployment insurance, which reads:
The cooperation of the provinces has been sought with a view to an amendment of the British North America Act which would empower the parliament of Canada to enact forthwith a national scheme of unemployment insurance. My ministers hope the proposal may meet with early approval in order that unemployment insurance legislation may be enacted during the present session of parliament.
That was a year ago. Since then it has developed, that three provinces, Alberta, Quebec, and New Brunswick, will not agree, and apparently the government are bogged down on unemployment insurance. Judging by the speech from the throne this year, it is now in the government's land of dreams; for we find this lone reference:
The government have not altered their view that a national unemployment insurance scheme is essential to a permanent policy of meeting the problem of unemployment.
Unemployment insurance will not settle the relief problem, but it will partly settle the problem of security for Canadian wage-earners, and it should not be delayed one day longer. There is no reason why Canada, with her progressive people, should lag behind the rest of the commonwealth in security legislation. I am afraid the main reason that such is the case is that we have the most out-ofdate government in the commonwealth.
My second suggestion is that the government have a committee of this house look into the possibility of extending old age pensions to Canadians between sixty-five and seventy years of age. It seems absurd to me to force people over sixty-five to work, with thousands of young people clamouring for work and unable to get a start in life. It may be that we would require a contributory scheme, but the whole question should be investigated and should be investigated now, not after the Rowell commission reports and not after the next election. In any event the government should stop the present tendency to treat those elder Canadians who apply for pension as paupers-which is an objectionable feature in the administration of the act at the present time, and very far removed from the original intention, which was that pensions should be a reward to pioneers.
As a third suggestion, I recommend that the government have part II of the National Housing Act amended at this session; that is, the part dealing with low rental housing. It

was passed last year with the best of intentions from all sides of the house. A $30,000,000 fund was provided, and yet not one dollar of that fund has been spent. Apparently this part of the act is a dud, and the reasons for that, at any rate in the city of Vancouver, are two. First of all, under the provisions of the act the taxes that a municipality levies must not exceed one per cent of the cost of construction. We have been met with the argument that it is unfair that a housing scheme in one block should be taxed only on the basis of one per cent whereas property across the street is taxed on the basis of, say four per cent. For that reason there is a strong objection to the act. The other objection is this: under the act rentals paid must cover carrying charges; for example, on a home which cost 82,400, the carrying charges amount to about $14 a month, so that that amount of rental must be collected; but then there is the further provision that the tenant cannot pay over one-fifth of the family income; this means that the income must be at least five times $14, which amounts to $70, so the lowest income group which can be helped must have an income of $70 a month, which amounts to about $850 a year. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are below that income group, probably all the people who need the help, so part II of the act is of no use to those who need it most, and in addition competes with the ordinary house owners who are desirous of renting their property.
I suggest that the act should be amended to meet these difficulties. I do not know just how it can be done-perhaps by providing that municipalities can tax up to two per cent, and certainly by giving the dominion power to make contributions to what is known as a rent reduction fund. At the present time only the municipalities and the provinces can contribute to such a fund.
There is great need of low rental housing in Canada. I do not want to take the time of the house, but I would quote briefly from the interim report of the national employment commission, which, at page 11, sets out the conditions very clearly. It is the report to the government made in July, 1937:
The commission recognized the desirability of a rounding out of governmental housing policy, particularly as regards accommodation for those unable themselves to afford an economic rent-often associated with slum clearance. Action in this field was considered necessary both from the viewpoint of eliminating a social sore all too prevalent, especially in the larger cities, and because of its effect in stimulating employment in the construction field.

The Address-Mr. Green
Then they go on to make this startling statement:
In making this recommendation the commission was influenced by the fact that Canadian governmental bodies had expended some $14,000,000 in 1930 to rent accommodation for relief recipients, and that in many instances such accommodation was unsanitary and unsuitable in the extreme. The commission feels that such a situation should not be allowed to continue in that it breeds conditions tending to increase unemployment by decreasing the employability of numbers of workers, thus making it harder for them to secure employment.
The fourth suggestion I would make is that the government follow the recommendation of its own national employment commission by setting up a national employment service in Canada. The present position is that the provinces have their employment agencies and the dominion subsidizes them to an aggregate sum of $150,000 a year. The commission found that these employment agencies are entirely inadequate. I should like to make it clear that I have nothing but praise for the personnel of the men in these employment agencies. They are not being given a chance to do the job. But this commission has found that our employment service is entirely inadequate. Appointed in June, 1936, it was only two months before the commission recommended to the government that these agencies should be administered by the nation. Five months later, in January, 1937, we find another emphatic recommendation that it was of vital importance that Canada should set up national employment agencies. Nothing was done in either case. Again, six months later, in July. 1937, we have the interim report of the commission, and I should like to read to hon. members one of the statements found at page 17 of that report:
Employment Service of Canada Early in the commission's investigations it became evident that the first and most vital step necessary to the successful handling of employment, re-employment and aid administration problems is the development of more efficient employment services throughout Canada. The present provincial employment services are in practice unfitted to meet the exigencies of the situation.
Again nothing was done, although the commission pleaded for action. In the final report, brought in a year ago-I believe it was a year ago to-day; no doubt members of the government will remember it very well-we find this further strong recommendation, one of the most emphatic recommendations of the commission. Dealing again with the national employment service it states at page 15:
The requirement here, as pointed out on page 19 of the interim report, is the prompt modernization and extension of the employment service of Canada, this with a view to a better linking together of employer and employee; to providing focal points for attacks on local employment problems, and as a means of gauging the relative degree of employability of those in receipt of aid. In discussions which the commission has had in recent months, general agreement has been expressed by all provincial governments as to the unsuitability of the existing set-up, and of the restricted services of the provincial employment services in fulfilling these vital functions.
The commission wishes to emphasize the urgency for action. It recommends that the service be placed immediately under the direction of the dominion government, both as to controlling principles and broad policies, but with provision for the appointment of strong regional directors, and regional advisory councils, to whom certain decentralized powers would be given, so as to ensure adequate weight being accorded, and attention being paid, to the problems peculiar to particular regions.
Similar advisory councils were used with great success under the home improvement plan.
Yet nothing has been done. Probably this is the worst example of drift by this government. The folly of such inaction is best shown by pointing to their fine youth program, for which I think the government are to be commended; yet there is no proper employment service to help these youths find jobs after they have completed their training. This condition is so bad that the minister of labour of British Columbia, Mr. Pearson, speaking in the provincial house last November, is reported by the Vancouver Province as saying:
"I'm not satisfied with the present set-up myself." . .	. When the federal government
proposed to take over the whole matter, in conjunction with unemployment insurance, he had had visions of an efficient employment service in charge of the provincial authorities, but had dropped it. He had waited in vain for Ottawa to act. Finally, he said, he had debated the matter of dominion and provincial em-' ployment service and last year decided the dominion intended to do nothing for the present, so set about his own reorganization plan.
"I started on the women's section, which needs reorganization more than the men's," Mr. Pearson stated. "I am going ahead," he said, "in spite of the indecision of Ottawa, and in the hope of permissive unemployment insurance in the provinces."
Then I suggest that the government follow the further recommendation of its own national employment commission, that through a national employment service the government take over the administration and payment of unemployment aid for all employables, as distinguished from unemployables, freeing the provinces and municipalities of this burden which certainly should not be the burden of the municipalities, because in the end that means .a burden on the homes of

The Address-Mr. Green
Canada. There is no reason why the municipalities should be responsible for the burden of such relief under the present tax set-up in Canada.
Meanwhile the government should do something about the problem of non-residents and migrants wandering by the thousands back and forth across this country. There are several steps the government could take. In the first place they could lay down uniform residence provisions. Each year a great deal of the money by way of grants-in-aid goes from the dominion government under agreements with the provincial governments. I suggest that in these agreements the government insert a provision that each province, in accepting the money, must adopt uniform residence standards so that we shall not have the present difficulty of one province insisting on two years' residence, another on three years, another on one year and so forth. This principle has been adopted in the agreement with British Columbia concerning municipalities in the province, by means of the following paragraph :
The province agrees to maintain such residence regulations that no person shall become ineligible to receive material aid by reason of having lost residence in one municipality or jurisdiction within the province before having established residence in another-
I say a similar provision should be written into the agreements to provide for regulations as between the provinces. Then the government should take full responsibility for the real migrants, those Canadians who cannot meet residential qualifications in any province; for those hundreds who really are not fit, the older men who are " burnt out," I suggest that the government set up farm hostels operated on a subsistence basis; certainly these men should be withdrawn from the employment market.
Another suggestion, which I particularly wish to present to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), is that the government should place far more emphasis upon the trans-Canada highway than they do at the present time. To me the trans-Canada highway means not only jobs in connection with construction; it also means jobs resulting from tourist traffic, and most important of all it means a wonderful way of promoting unity in Canada. Anyone coming from the more remote provinces of Canada cannot fail to be impressed by that argument. If this highway is completed it will give thousands of Canadians, who otherwise could not get it, an opportunity to travel across their own country and to meet and understand their fellow-Canadians. I would point out that at the present time there are two gaps in the trans-Canada highway. In British Columbia there is a small gap known

as the Big Bend gap; but in the northern part of this great province of Ontario there is a gap of about 250 miles, with very little apparent effort to have that gap completed. Someone suggests that is due to failure to agree with Mitch, and that may explain a lot. But surely it is not too much to ask or expect that action should be taken, and at this session; and in that connection I should like to remind the house of the policy of the National Conservative party on this project:
The National Conservative party reaffirms its policy of completing the construction of and the future maintenance of a trans-Canada highway from coast to coast as a national undertaking.
If this government does not hurry up and do that this year, it will not get a chance to do it at all.
My final suggestion is that this country this year should accept full responsibility for its veterans who served in France or another theatre of war and who are at the present time on the relief rolls across the country. In other words, I believe Canada should accept responsibility for its fighting men. I do not think there are many people in Canada to-night who would not say heartily that this responsibility rests right here, with the dominion government. Yet year after year we have been unable to get the government to take any action. They have taken the responsibility for the unfit man, but they will not assume responsibility for the fit veteran who wants to work but is unable to find employment. That is the stand of the government despite the recommendations of the Hyndman committee as far back as 1935 and the recommendations of its own Rattray commission in 1937 and again in the final report of 1938. I should like to refresh the memory of hon. gentlemen with regard to the recommendations of that commission, which are to be found at page 63 of the report:
. . . the commission has come to the conclusion that it can do no less than recommend that the dominion government accept responsibility for all indigent unemployed veterans who were domiciled in Canada at date of enlistment and who saw service in a theatre of actual war.
There are only about ten thousand of them, according to the commission, so it is not as though there were hundreds of thousands of these men to be provided for. The reasons given by the commission for that recommendation still hold good, and have not been answered by this government. One reason, for example, is that the average age of these men is about fifty years. What possible chance under present conditions has a veteran fifty years of age of finding employment? It has been found further that these men are pre-aged, that they have suffered through loss

The Address-Mr. Dujjus
of training during their younger years when they were serving at the front, and that they are a marginal group on the labour market; in other words, that they can work for only a few months or a few weeks at a time. The commission also found a fact which every hon. member knows to be true, that the tendency of the municipalities and the provinces is to say to those veterans on relief, "Oh, you belong to the dominion government; what are you bothering us for? It is not up to us to look after you. You should be cared for by the dominion government." The final and the most telling reason given by the Rattray commission is this, as it appears at page 40 of the report:
We feel, as we are confident the country at large feels, that no matter what Canada has done to requite the services of her veterans, her obligation to them is not discharged while one of them walks the streets vainly in search of work, or while one of them is in distress.
These men served Canada. We were proud of the word "Canada" on our shoulder-straps. We were not serving British Columbia, Ontario. Prince Edward Island or any single province; we were serving Canada. The responsibility for the care of those fighting men rests with the Canadian government, and the form the assistance to be given them should take is a matter for the government to decide. They may adopt the recommendation of the commission for a provisional economic allowance, or they might consider an extension of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. The point is that the responsibility rests right here.
In conclusion, may I say that all these are problems within Canada. The government has its precious trade treaty. Now let it get down to business at home. Let it face these vital issues now, in the 1939 session. Canada cannot afford to lose these years for development, for progress and for bringing greater happiness to her people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) does not expect me to follow him in all his arguments, much less to agree with them. At the outset I desire to join hon. members in paying my humble tributes to the hon. members for Essex West (Mr. McLarty) and Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) upon their elevation to the cabinet. I am confident both of these gentlemen will do great honour and credit to themselves, their constituents and the government of Canada.
One of the reasons I have sought the indulgence of the house at this time is that I do not wish the opposition groups to conclude that because I occupy a seat on this
side of the chamber I am in agreement with their philosophies, their theories or even their bitter criticism of the government and the splendid legislation it has brought down.
In order to do my part towards making it possible for the house to prorogue prior to the royal visit, which I believe should be the aim of all hon. members, I shall be as brief as possible.
With what has been so eloquently said by previous speakers of the great honour to be conferred upon the people of Canada by the proposed visit of Their Royal Majesties King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, I am in full accord. I am sure the committee which has this important matter in hand will arrange for and extend to their royal majesties a very cordial welcome and fitting reception.
I wish also to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) and the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) upon their excellent speeches in moving and seconding the address in reply. Each acquitted himself in a very creditable and dignified manner. I desire also to take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate most heartily the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon the honour which has come to him upon being elected leader of the National Conservative party and of His Majesty's loyal opposition.
Permit me to refer, with a limited amount of pardonable pride to the constituency of Peterborough West which I have the honour to represent, a constituency comprising the industrial city of Peterborough, one of the finest cities in Canada; Lakefield, the "village beautiful" on the Trent waterway; the fertile township of South Monaghan lying "sunny side up" on the shore of Rice lake in Northumberland county, and eight townships dotted with lakes and rivers in the county of Peterborough. The residents of the agricultural area of that constituency, in their efforts in advanced agriculture, have achieved many outstanding records in dairying, live stock, grain and other products.
I believe I can give the house a concrete example of how a judicious management of public affairs can bring about happiness, economy and increasing confidence. During and subsequently to the war, the city of Peterborough looked to the future with a determination to reduce debt. For several years past the city has not issued any debentures. It has, moreover, paid out of current revenue all relief costs, and in addition has gradually reduced its mill rate.
The net debt of the city of Peterborough at the end of 1933 was $3,145,900. In the intervening years this amount has been reduced
The Address-Mr. Duffus

The Address-Mr. Duflus

If we approach this question nationally, from the standpoint of labour, it is estimated, taking the generally accepted basis that eighty per cent of the cost of construction goes to labour directly or indirectly, that new home-building activity financed under the dominion housing legislation accounts to date for a payment to labour of approximately $29,000,000; and if advances of over $24,000,000 under the home improvement plan are also taken into account, it is evident that the combined total has provided for the payment to labour of a sum amounting to date to about $53,000,000. This is a formidable figure, and the expenditure of this amount has obviously greatly assisted labour, notwithstanding the criticism of hon. members opposite.
In view of the extremely rapid increase not only in the number of loans being negotiated but in the increasing number of municipalities all over Canada that are taking advantage of the benefits of the National Housing Act, it is difficult even to hazard a conjecture as to what the increased activities of the construction industry will be during this and following years. It may indeed tax our lumber and building material industries to the limit.
Speaking of the basic industry of agriculture, which all hon. members admit is the bedrock foundation of stable prosperity for all our industries, it must be obvious to all that the Anglo-United-States-Canada treaty, with its great possibilities of increasing world's markets, was designed also for the purpose of giving our farmers the assistance which they so greatly need and to which they are justly entitled. I should like to make some extensive observations in respect of agriculture, but time will not permit.
Farmers are the founders of civilization. Moie and more agriculture is honoured with a pi ice among the sciences. It is a science of necessity, a science which has stood the test of ages. Our country's weal and woe depend absolutely upon agriculture and the farmer. Empires have risen and crumbled into dust; various arts have been learned and forgotten; but agriculture still survives. Many nations owe their life and progressive advancement to the character of their agriculturists. Amidst all the mechanical skill that has characterized nations, agriculture has held a distinguished position. The happiest days of ancient Rome were marked by agricultural prosperity. When Italy was in danger, consequent upon the evil of civil wars, every effort was made to restore that noble art in order to rescue her from ruin. In the primeval ages agriculture was the commodity parent of traffic. To-day it is still essential for the promotion of trade

in general. If all our mines of gold and silver became exhausted, our commerce with all nations prohibited; if all art were abolished, the fertility of the land alone would supply sustenance for the people of the earth.
May I express the confident hope that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his colleagues will continue their efforts toward bettering the lot of those without whom it would be impossible to find a means of sustaining the teeming millions of the world. In this connection I suggest that the government give consideration to the advisability of bringing down during this session, legislation, such as exists in some of the provinces, with a view to controlling the orderly marketing of all farm products.
In view of the successful efforts of the government in so many directions it is little wonder that there is increasing confidence in the minds of the people of Canada. Canada's Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), with his fine sense of constitutional accuracies, has always served the best interests of Canada, Britain and the British commonwealth of nations, with unparalleled distinction. His expressed determination that a strong, united empire is the best guarantee of world peace at a time when communism and other isms are so prevalent is recognized throughout the world. The enhancement of national unity, the demolition of sectional barriers, the stimulation of a deeper spirit of community interests and all his utterances, both in parliament and out of it, reveal a conspicuous consistency of policy resulting in the present government enlisting a continually widening circle of favour in the dominion. When Canadian history is written, our present Prime Minister will come into his own as a prime minister whose achievements do not deserve him to be ranked less than Canada's most outstanding statesman among those who have preceded him.
Speaking before the press after the session in 1936 the late Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden said:
Dunning is a splendid fellow, the highest type of public man, who enjoys the confidence of his countrymen, and well may they be glad that he has charge of a department of such tremendous responsibility in these critical days.
And further, " Young men of promise " was his description of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers); the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe); the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power); and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). What Sir Robert said in respect of these hon. gentlemen in my humble opinion applies equally to the other members of the cabinet, including the two new appointees.

The Address-Mr. Warren
How fortunate we are to have such able administrators at a time when there is so much economic and social turmoil throughout the world.- But for them we could not sustain the huge increase in trade that Canada has enjoyed, such an expansion of international activity in commerce and industry as producing and earning Canadians hope for and are now enjoying in large measure.
I wonder if we who live in Canada have anything like a full appreciation of the advantages we enjoy-the freedom, liberty and security that are ours-in comparison with what people in other countries of the world have to endure who live in constant suspense, in those lands where people go to bed at night not knowing whether they will see the morning and, if they do see it, whether in the morning earth and sky will be darkened by approaching death.
Divine Providence has surely blessed our country in many different ways when we consider her wealth in agriculture, mines, forests, and fisheries, her vast resources of water power, her grain and fruit land, her unimpaired freedom of three oceans, and last and most important of all, the character of her people.
I believe I am within the bounds of moderation when I say that history does not reveal a finer example of good will and friendship between Iwo great nations than that existing between Canada and the United States of America. By common consent, on both sides of the border, we recognize a permanent pact of two peoples sealed by upwards of one hundred years of history and deriving its authority from the mutual good will of these people rather than from exchange of diplomatic pledges. Canadians sometimes think the United States fails to comprehend the political structure of the empire. To dream of a commonwealth of nations that will some day take in the United States of America is perhaps to dream too greatly.
In the meantime, it is much to know that on all vital matters, in nearly all the supreme things of life, the heart of the great nation to the south of us does beat with the empire, holds her common ideals, common aspirations, common truths.
Mr. Speaker, in the maintenance of that free harmony in the years ahead lies much of the future goodwill of the world.

Mr. R. M. WARREN (Renfrew North); In my contribution to this debate I shall dispense with the preliminaries except to say that I heartily agree with the sentiments so ably expressed by so many hon. members in appreciation of the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I want also to extend to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) my congratulations upon his elevation to office as leader of the National Conservative party. I would also extend a word of welcome to the new members: the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), and the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Bercovitch). I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. McLarty) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) upon their elevation to cabinet positions in this government.
A great variety of subjects has been discussed in this debate. This parliament is blessed or cursed with having three groups on the opposition benches. Many speakers, particularly on the other side of the house, appear to consider it as one of their first duties to make the efforts of the government appear futile and unavailing. The reading public, if they do not use their own judgment, must receive the impression that we are surely living in a land of misery, hardship and unhappiness. My effort will be to attempt to introduce a note of optimism among so many speeches of a pessimistic nature.
This government, during their three years of office, have devoted a great deal of attention to the development of trade and the negotiating of fair trade agreements with any countries which are willing to trade with us. In this they have been singularly successful. That is very well illustrated by comparing our trade figures of 1938 with those of 1934. In 1934 our imports amounted to $513,000,000 and our exports to $660,000,000; in 1938 our exports had risen to $956,000,000 and our imports to $677,000,000, being an
The Address-Mr. Warren

increase of 44-85 per cent in our exports and of 31-97 per cent in our imports. Recently we have seen negotiated new agreements between the United States and Canada and between the United States and Great Britain. I believe I could not do better in the way of expressing the feeling of the farmers generally throughout Canada regarding this treaty than to quote from the speech of the hon. member for Brandon:
Experienced cattle dealers have told me that they have found a distinctly healthier tone in the cattle market ever since this agreement was announced. These men are convinced, after years of experience, -that the tariff reductions and the increased quota admissible to the United States, now 225,000 head, will mean a very decided impetus to our live stock development. An alert business man with an analytical complex remarked to me a few days before I left for Ottawa that, having studied this agreement, he had come to the conclusion that it was the smartest-that is the word he used-piece of business legislation enacted in Canada since confederation.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that it is also quite true to say that our lumbermen are quite optimistic respecting the improvement of their industry as a result of this new trade agreement. If all governments throughout the world would follow the example of the Canadian government in their endeavour to negotiate and carry out fair trade agreements, would this not go a long way toward solving the problems of the world?
One of the favourite topics in this debate has been unemployment. I wish to deal with it for a few minutes, although I am not sure that I shall be able to offer the government any new suggestions regarding it. The government has been deluged with advice, some of it good and some not so good. I feel that the handling of this problem is just as safe in the hands of this government as it would be in the hands of any body of men whom the Canadian people could elect.
In discussing this question we ought to keep in mind that, compared with the figures during the lean years of the Bennett-Manion regime, we have reduced unemployment by approximately 50 per cent. If we can accomplish that within the space of three years, what may not be done within the space of six years? With the same amount of progress our problem would be entirely solved in another three years.
I desire to inject a note of cheer into a debate which has fairly bristled with pessimism. If we get one cheerful speech from the government side of the house, it is followed by three speeches from the opposition benches where the speakers vie with each other to paint as black a picture as possible. I say as a new member that this has a most de-

pressing effect. I am not worried about the effect it has on us in this house; what troubles me is the effect that it does and must have on citizens generally throughout the dominion. Of all the orations of gloom to which we have been permitted to listen, none excelled that of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). When he reached his climax and was so ably describing the actions which he considered should be taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as captain of the ship of state, it did seem rather a pity that his speech was more or less spoiled by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser), interjecting the remark that the hon. member for Kootenay East ought to know, for he had scuttled one ship.
But I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) in reference to the difficulties of our farmers. While he was speaking, my mind went back a few years to the time when he and the present leader of the opposition were sitting on the treasury benches, forming part of the government of this country. I remembered that we sold hogs on the Montreal market for $3.85 per 100 pounds, and the finest finished cattle for as low as $3 per 100 pounds. I compared that in my mind with conditions to-day, and recalled that this week hogs sold on the Montreal market for $9.75 per 100 pounds and finished cattle for S7 per 100 pounds, an improvement of considerably more than 100 per cent in the prices paid for these two important products of the farm. I am sure even the hon. member for Kootenay East should agree that the picture is scarcely as black as he would have us believe.
But, Mr. Speaker, this wail of woe comes regularly, without variation, from a number of hon. members from Alberta. Listening to their speeches one would think that in their beautiful province the birds never sing, the clouds have no silver lining, the sun never shines and the flowers never bloom; that they have nothing at all in that wonderful province to be thankful for. But is the situation as bad as all that? They have almost limitless areas of perhaps the most fertile and productive land in the world; they have lakes and rivers; they have timber resources; they have so much coal that you can shovel it out of the hillsides; they have an almost inexhaustible supply of oil; they have railroads and bus lines and beautiful cities-a great, youthful, growing nation-in itself. Even this year there was a building boom in the city of Edmonton. They have flocks and herds, which carry off prizes in any competition, and then they always have the hope that one of these days

The Address-Mr. Warren
each person will receive a monthly cheque of $25, which, indeed, must be comforting to the people of that province.
It is quite true that each province has its troubles; but troubles and difficulties do not hurt us if we develop the ability to overcome our troubles and surmount our difficulties. It is true that we have our problem of the single transient, but we had that in normal times. We have our single, homeless men in every community, but why do we hear so much about it to-day? One reason is that under the Bennett-Manion regime the then administration instituted the idea that it was the duty of the government to look after these men. When I hear this question being discussed, I always think of the single, homeless men in my own community. I suppose they are in every community, men who came from the old country as boys, who have grown up and have no place they can call home, though many of them have established themselves. I recall that in lean times, a few years ago, these boys would wander away from our community. They would ride the rods; they would try the slave camps, but they would always come back, always without a dollar; and I never knew one of those boys in our community who did not come back to find an open door waiting for him, with a farmer offering him wages to help on the farm. It is true that at times the wages may have been small, but I always noticed that when one farmer was finished with one of those fellows invariably there was another farmer waiting to give him a job.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) rather sarcastically referred to what he called a soup-kitchen in Winnipeg, where he told us three thousand men were being fed. I was in Winnipeg at that soup-kitchen when harvesting and threshing were in full swing in Manitoba, and when there was plenty of work. Why, even the high school boys were in the harvest fields; but as I was shown the splendid way they feed those men who call themselves single, homeless transients, it seemed to me like a great haven of rest for men who were too tired to go out and fork sheaves to a separator or follow a binder.

Evidently the people of that territory, as well as their member, have retained their pioneer spirit and stick to the old truth that if a man will not work neither shall he eat.
I was greatly interested in an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 23. Evidently there had been some dispute between a gentleman named Tom Moore and Doctor Putman, a controller in the civic government of Ottawa. Doctor Putman had suggested that Mr. Moore was complaining about the hundreds of skilled men who are not able to find employment, and made a suggestion that Mr. Moore should organize a cooperative building association among those skilled mechanics who are idle. Doctor Putman said, in part:
Find an architect, a business manager, carpenters, bricklayers, plasterers, plumbers, painters and labourers. Let these idle tradesmen build half a dozen semi-detached houses on city owned lots. I will do my utmost to persuade the city to supply all material. When the houses are completed the city will sell them at auction, deduct half the assessed value of the land and the total cost of materials and hand over to Mr. Moore the balance for distribution among the workmen.
I was not particularly interested in that part of the article. The following is the part of the article which attracted my attention:
Doctor Putman goes on to say he doubts if Mr. Moore knew what he actually said in council or why he felt called upon to say anything. He explains he did so because other speakers in council were giving an impression that "Canada had quite gone to the dogs," that there was no work, young people were in despair, faced the future without hope, that someone, presumably the city council, ought to find jobs for the thousands of fully trained and highly efficient young folk who were eating their hearts out in idleness.
Then Doctor Putman is reported as saying:
Now to my mind, we have had during the past two years, too much preaching of this pessimistic nonsense. Some of it comes from leaders of youth, some from social workers, some from the pulpit, some from the press and, much of it from cheap politicians. But whatever its source the effect is vicious. It leads youth to think they are victims of circumstances which they cannot control. It tends to make sour their attitude toward society and
The Address-Mr. Warren

toward our political and economic structure. It tends to make them lean upon the oars at a time when they ought to lend every effort toward pushing their boat against the stream.
Then the article states:
Canadians held half a continent and numbered eleven millions. There was everything needed to create a paradise on earth, millions of acres of fertile soil only half cultivated, rich deposits of economic and precious minerals, valuable clays, rivers, lakes and sea coasts teeming with fish, fertile protected valleys for raising fruit, great areas of waste lands ready to grow more forests, rich swamp lands begging to be drained. What more could a people ask?
The sun shone, showers descended, grass grew, flowers and fruit ripened, animals thrived, with sheep giving wool, cows giving milk, hens laying eggs, bees gathering honey. What more could the Lord give a people? Whose fault was it if some went hungry and half naked and lived in shacks? Surely it was the fault of the people themselves. Any man who said youth had no chance was ignorant and a worker of mischief.
Doctor Putman challenged his critic to point to any country where youth had a better chance.
Was it Germany, Italy, China, Japan or Russia? Or would it be Belgium. Holland or Scandinavia where youths worked long hours for a pittance and ate meat once or twice a week.
This is the spirit of the rural districts, the spirit of the villages, and to a lesser extent, the spirit of the towns. Unfortunately, however, it can scarcely be said to be the spirit of the cities, as expressed by gatherings of mayors who get together to urge that the federal government ought to take over one hundred per cent of the responsibility for relief.
This statement coming from an official of a civic government was to me just like a balmy breeze in the midst of a blizzard. In the rural parts we have our needy; but how do we take care of them? We look after them in the old-fashioned way; the neighbours assist, and the churches help. We have managed to get along in that way. Is it any wonder that we resented the suggestion of the present leader of the opposition who, in his speech at Barry's Bay shortly after his election, said it ought to be the duty of the federal government to bear the whole cost of relief. If we take away all the responsibility from local municipalities, and remove all the incentive on their part to get rid of the burden of relief-

But it was "remarkable" how the economio structure withstood depressing influences. Occasionally someone breaks into print with a statement that the church and democracy have failed. At this point I should like to pay tribute to the work of the churches in the district with which I am best acquainted.
I do not confine my tribute to any particular denomination. During the past lean years ministers and priests alike have distinguished themselves in helping the needy and trying to solve this problem with which we are faced. I have in mind an Irish priest in Renfrew county in whose parish an agitation had occurred for the distribution of relief. One Sunday morning this priest preached a sermon. in the course of which he told his congregation that there would be no relief in his parish. There was no relief and they got along nicely without it. These ministers and priests are still carrying on. When the statement is made that the church has failed or that democracy has failed, quite often no thought is given to the good things with which we are surrounded.
I have noticed that there appears to be an awakening among our younger men, our younger business and professional men. They appear to be more ready to enter into local activities, and there seems to be a keen desire on their part to render service to their communities. It seems to me that with the cooperation of labour, and with a more fearless and aggressive attitude on the part of employers of labour who might make an effort to employ a greater number of labourers, we in this dominion can surmount our difficulties and solve our problems.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to follow the hon. member who has preceded me (Mr. Warren) in extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Matthews) and the seconder (Mr. Chevrier) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne by his excellency to this House of Commons. I desire also to extend my congratulations to the newly appointed cabinet ministers. I am sure we have every reason to expect that they will represent us as ably as those ministers already appointed to a cabinet which is considered to be one of the most brilliant Canada has ever had.
I desire also to extend my congratulations to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his appointment as head of what is now termed the National Conservative party. He has been receiving so many congratulations lately that he hardly pays any attention to them, but I do want him to know that mine are sincere. I have heard my own leader say that if you want to know what the future has in store for you, you will
be wise to take a glimpse at the past. With this thought in mind I have a few kindly suggestions to make to my hon. friend. The Conservative party is very rich in leaders and ex-leaders. I think we shall have to give them at least that much of a break. There are also triplets of would-be leaders, and it will be interesting to watch just what they are going to accomplish in their respective departments. I am of the opinion that the people of Canada, if they look back over the road they have travelled, will be extremely reluctant to place any great responsibility on the shoulders of these hon. gentlemen. I am sure the Canadian people have learned their lesson, and will realize just what problems each of these ex-leaders has left upon the door-steps of the Canadian people.
If we go back into history for a period of twenty-four years, I think we can discover something of the record of the ex-leaders of the Conservative party. Every one of these ex-leaders has left a national problem upon the door-steps of the Canadian people, and I am inclined to the view that this is the reason why they have adopted the name of National Conservative party. In the first place they left us a national debt. During the past twenty-four years there have been twelve years of Conservative administration and twelve years of Liberal administration. During the twelve years of Conservative administration there were deficits totalling $2,441,700,000. The combined deficits of twelve years of Conservative administration amounted to that astronomical sum. During the twelve years of Liberal administration there were deficits totalling $235,000,000, but during that time there were seven years of surpluses which totalled $310,000,000. There was a credit balance in favour of the Liberals amounting to about $75,000,000, representing a reduction in our national debt in consequence of Liberal administration.
I was greatly interested on Sunday night in listening to the radio address of Mr. Mc-Cullagh, the publisher of the Globe and Mail. He stressed, quite rightly, the importance of the national debt. He emphasized the fact that so much of the Canadian taxpayers' money was used to carry our national debt. There were many observations which Mr. McCullagh made with which I agreed heartily. I am inclined to the view that he is doing a worthy act by directing the attention of the people to the serious situation that exists. But I want the people to understand the true condition of affairs, so that by taking a look back into the past they may be able to guide and direct their actions in the future. I would
The Address-Mr. Wood

say to the leader of the opposition that he and his trio can never expect to win the confidence of the people.
Around 1917 or 1918, when the leader of the opposition was a supporter of the government of that day, we had inflicted upon us another national problem in the form of the Canadian National Railways. Not that I am saying that the intentions were not good, and undoubtedly the Canadian National Railways has given a wonderful service to this dominion. I believe, moreover, that it never gets a fair deal in the press, which is inclined to expose all the shortcomings of the system without giving it credit for the many contributions it has made to the national life of this country. But I can never understand why a company that goes insolvent, when it is taken over by the government as the national railways, was not purchased for what it was worth without all its obligations being assumed. I believe that if we had had sound business administration at that time, the Canadian National Railways would not be the menace to the prosperity of the Canadian people that some are saying it is to-day. So far as I personally am concerned, I rather defend the Canadian National Railways because, although they have a deficit of around one million dollars a week, we must consider the services rendered by the system. It gives us the cheapest freight rate of any transportation system in the world, a rate of less than 98 cents per ton-mile, which I do not think can, at the present time, be paralleled by any other transportation system on this continent..
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure but that the competitive railway to the Canadian National Railways may be costing us just as much as the Canadian National Railways when one takes into consideration the contributions which the country has made in subsidies to the privately-owned road. I had occasion to refer to the 1938 Year Book, and I saw at page 649 that we have granted in subsidies to the Canadian National Railways, prior to the amalgamation, 898,000,000, and to the Canadian Pacific Railway, 8119,000,000; the Canadian National Railways were granted land subsidies of 7,640,000 acres, while the Canadian Pacific Railway was granted 36,956,000 acres. So I really do not believe that the head of the Canadian Pacific Railway has reason to complain very much of the cost to the Canadian people of the Canadian National system. When you sum it all up, I am not so sure but that the Canadian Pacific Railway may be just as guilty of bearing down heavily upon the people of Canada.
I do not wish to be misunderstood. I do not wish it to be thought that I do not view seriously the deficits on our national railway 
system. On the contrary I believe that every effort should be made to wipe off that deficit. But there are certain facts that I believe should be brought to the attention of the Canadian people. There is the fact that 83 per cent of the stockholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway live outside Canada; and the fact that 75 per cent of the bondholders of the Dominion of Canada live within Canada is one indication that we ought to move very cautiously in doing anything that might interfere with the credit of this dominion in regard to those bonds. So much for the second national problem that was left to us by a Conservative administration.
I come now to the national problem of unemployment, which is considered Canada's greatest national problem. In 1930 we were told by the then leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) that if we elected his party to office he was going to cure unemployment or perish in the attempt. I am not doubting at all the sincerity of the predecessor of the present leader of the opposition. In my association with him in the last three years I came to admire him very much. Have we made any progress in that regard?
In 1935, the year before the present administration came into power, our exports amounted to $69.11 per capita. In 1937 they had risen to $96.23. In 1938, according to the estimate of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), and assuming our population to be still eleven millions, our export trade had receded slightly to $88 per capita. How does that compare with the export trade of other countries? Great Britain's export trade amounted to $56.83 per capita, and the United States, a country which hon. gentlemen opposite always hold up as an example, and which they try to follow in their policy of ex-clusionist tariffs, had an export trade amounting to $25.83 per capita. Compare that with our $88 per capita in 1938. That seems to me convincing evidence that a reasonable amount of progress has been made.
After all, the success of any country depends largely upon the prosperity of its internal industries. Money is timid, and if there is anything a man will fight for it is probably the little bit of savings he has. In my opinion it is extremely necessary, even though the leader of the social credit party (Mr. Blackmore) will not agree with me, that money should receive its fair share of reward in our economic life. Let me point out what industry has contributed to the prosperity of the country. In 1935, total dividends paid out
by industry amounted to $222,629,000, and in 1938, that had gone up to $315,000,000, or an increase of almost S100,000,000. That represents what industry received as the reward of its efforts. I am not so sure that the employment of labour has wholly kept pace with the rewards of industry, but I might point to another record I have from the bureau of industries-and this relates to my own constituency in particular.
I have the honour to represent a part of the city of Brantford, and so I take this opportunity to show what progress has been made in Brantford city and in the town of Paris. I find that the total number of employees in Brantford in 1935 was 6,002, and in 1936 the number had gone up to 6,384, a pretty fair increase for one year. And what about the wage bill? The wage bill had increased in one year, under Liberal administration, $660,000. Take next the town of Paris, with a population of 4,000. There has been an increase of employees from 1.151, to 1,221. with an increase of $158,219 in the wage bill. And that is only one year. I am satisfied that the figures for 1937 will show a large increase and 1938 will be a long way ahead of 1935.
I have under my hand a bulletin published by the commissioner of the city of Brantford, and I find recorded therein that in two and a half years fifteen new industries have been started-not very large, because all the industries in that community start on a small scale. In that community, if there are any savings the people try to put them back into industry so as to develop an industrial organization that will create goods and services for the people. I do not think we have any reason to be downcast. We are making progress. After listening to the pessimistic speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, who are always looking down, who have their noses in the gutter all the time, stirring up filth, and who, if there is anything wrong, are great artists in throwing it into our faces, I think it is time to call attention to some of the nice things in this dominion.
For instance, consider the fact that we stand fourth among the exporting nations of1 the world. We were in the sixth place in 1935; today we are fourth, and though it is true that in 1938 exports may have declined to some extent, it must be remembered that we had a poor crop in 1937. Surely there must be something in the Canadian people; surely there must be some good in the administration of the affairs of the country, when we have been able to find markets and have risen to the fourth place among the nations of the world in selling the products of our
The Address-Mr. Wood

labour. These are facts that cannot be denied, and I would ask the leader of the opposition and his followers to peruse these figures carefully and to see if they can honestly rise in their places in this house and indulge in criticism.
Our national debt, it is true, is considerable, but the Liberal party is not responsible for the great portion of it. In 1935 the national debt of the United States was much lower relatively than the national debt of Canada, but to-day our debt is $23 per capita less than the debt in the United States. It has generally been characteristic of our Conservative friends opposite, on all occasions, to hold up the United States as an example, to refer to that country's tariff and the way in which its affairs are administered. But when it comes to an election, those same gentlemen opposite have a way of wrapping themselves up in the flag of loyalty and talking imperialism as though they had a monopoly of the loyalty of Canada. The Liberals, however, prefer, in the matter of administration, to follow the British policy rather than that of the United States. While conditions have been depressed in the past year, if we take into consideration internal and external trade we shall find that Canada's trade has receded only 16 per cent, whereas the trade of the United States has receded 46 per cent. It shows that the Canadian economy is so built up by wise administration as to be able to withstand the impact of conditions such as we have had to face in the past year. These are things the people have a right to know.
At this point I should like to quote a famous authority on trade. I do not want to take up the time of the house in reading extracts, because I do not like to read either my own speeches or the opinions of others. What I have to say is the product of my own mind. I represent the people of Brant; I believe that they sent me here to give expression to the views which I think they hold; and I have always endeavoured to follow that rule. I shall, however, depart from it on this occasion to quote briefly an opinion expressed by Sir George Paish, who has been quoted before. He says:
Progress has brought railways, steamships, motor cars, airplanes, telephones, telegraphs and the radio. All countries are joined together into a single unit. Why should not each part of the world give what it can to the welfare of the entire world? The result would be amazing prosperity.
Bear in mind, there is no limit to the possible trade of the world. I am convinced that as soon as we can get things on to the right lines, there will be an expansion of trade such as we have not even dreamed of. There is not one physical thing lacking to bring about a vast expansion of trade. The only thing lacking is mental capacity and courage.

The first, and vital, thing is that the nations should trade freely with each other. There is no doubt about it.
The second thing is, again open money markets to the capital and credit needs of the world. You cannot have prosperity unless capital and credit are freely available. The difference between periods of prosperity and periods of depression during the past century came through the fact that when there was confidence, and capital and credit were flowing freely, you had active trade, and when there was no confidence and no movement of capital and credit there were trade depressions.
I am satisfied that if our good friends opposite would be more cautious; if they would refrain from undue criticism and not try to undermine the morale of the people, and if my good friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and of the Social Credit party would desist from preaching their unsound theories, we should find that money which is now hidden would soon be brought out and would be invested in industry, with the result that there would be an enhanced standard of living, a standard higher even than it is to-day.
I notice that the other day the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Poole) made some rather extravagant remarks with regard to the integrity of hon. members on this side of the house, suggesting that every time they voted they must have qualms of conscience. Perhaps he can tell me how a man can conscientiously issue a cheque, knowing that he has nothing in the bank with which to meet it. That is absolutely the theory of social credit; they want to issue money upon the credit of the country, upon its natural resources. But I know that if I issue my cheque and sign my name to it, and have no funds in the bank, there is no use in my telling the judge when I go before him that "I intended to have some here," or "I expect to have a good crop and in two or three years I shall have some money and you can cash my cheque on that." But that, as I see it, is exactly social credit, and nothing else.

I was brought up in a home where life and religion were taken seriously, where I was taught that wealth was the result and product of labour; that only by the application of labour to our natural resources could you get any results, and that you could not get them before you applied the labour. Failure to

The Address-Mr. Wood
recognize that is one of the reasons why we are suffering to-day. I am inclined to take the view that if we had all our people employed in creating national wealth, our difficulties would be solved.
