speechtext: Why does not the hon. member employ them, then?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why does not the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) hire one of them?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Personally I am employing all I can afford to employ. As the hon. member has raised the question, let me say that I believe it is the duty of those of us who are in a position to employ labour to endeavour to do so. I commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for having drawn attention the other day to that point. Industry must rise to the occasion. I have drawn attention to the fact that they have received this year in dividends around 8319,000,000, and I believe it is their duty to put into employment some of the unemployed men in their particular communities.
I remember that when I was a boy my father spoke of a depression which existed in the early nineties. At that time 60 per cent of the population of the dominion lived on farms and only 40 per cent in the cities. What happened? Did the farmers put these men on relief? No; during the winter these men snuggled in, did chores and cut wood so that they would start at least on equal terms the next spring, go out to work for eight months and get wages. But we have lost that pioneer spirit. Until we get back to some of the sober realities of life, we shall never come out of this depression. You cannot continue to mollycoddle people and give them something for nothing. I am inclined to think that it is just as wrong to take money from some people and hand it to others without any return, as it is to take something for nothing.
I notice that the service clubs have taken a great interest in the problem of unemployed youth. I believe that if they would organize in various cities and endeavour to meet the needs of these people, there are many things they could do. So far as men with money are concerned, there are plenty of farms they could buy, and they could put some of these men now on relief upon the farms. This would increase the value of the farms, and I believe those who took this course would eventually be rewarded. But if people who have means do not rise to the occasion and make some voluntary effort towards the employment of the unfortunate people in the cities, I hate to think what the future has in
store for us. If the unemployed continue to increase, they will eventually have power and will attempt to try out some of the isms which are advocated by our friends opposite. The advocates of these isms may be sincere. I am not going to question their sincerity-I think a great deal of these hon. members personally -but I know what would happen if ever their isms were put into effect. There has always been a group of people who are never satisfied with the existing condition of affairs; not that they ever do anything to make them better, but they have acquired the habit of finding fault with everything, of always looking down in the gutter to find something wrong. You may change your economic system-as far as I am concerned I do not care what kind of system we have; I made a living in the past and can make one in the future-but you would have the same people then complaining about the new economic system who are complaining about the present one; for if you have it in you, you are going to rise to the top, no matter what kind of system is in operation; and if you have not, the only thing those who are more fortunate can do is to take you by the hand and help you along.
A great deal has been said with regard to the unfortunate position we are supposed to be in. While I am making an honest defence of the government, I am not saying that everything is right. Everything never was right. But I do believe it would be wise for us to draw attention to some of the good things we have to-day. Something has been said about the standard of living. In my view there is no such thing as "a" standard of living; we have eleven million people and eleven million standards of living. Be that as it may, let me remark that there are some men who would get 820 a week and by the time they were fifty years old would be prosperous; others, although receiving the same income, would always be poor. So I do not believe there is any way of defining what a standard of living is. The fact of the matter is that the Canadian people to-day have the highest standard of living of any country in the world; I do not think we need take second place even to the United States. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that for every eight people in the Dominion of Canada there is a car or a truck? You could load everybody in the dominion in a car or truck and get them right out of this country without making a second trip. In only one other country can that be done, and that is the United States; they have one car or truck to five people.
It may be our good friends across the way would like to go to Russia or Spain or some other country and enjoy the fruits of the economic system there. In Russia, where one
The Address-Mr. Wood

rides one hundred and fifty walk; in Germany, where one rides ten walk. The hon. member for Red Deer made allusion to the fact that Germany did not have any unemployment, and recommended that we take a leaf out of Germany's book. Let us admit they have no unemployment in Germany, but neither have we any forced labour or compulsory military service to keep our people employed. I think hon. members should be very cautions about making such statements. In the constituency that I represent, Brant, there are more cars registered than there are in some of the countries of central Europe.
We ought to appreciate some of the good things we have in Canada. There is a radio in practically every second home in the dominion. We enjoy many of the luxuries of life which are not obtainable in other countries, and I think it will be just as wise if, instead of refusing to show appreciation of the advantages we have, we take into consideration some of the blessings we enjoy. The fact is that we have so many blessings and such a high standard of living that we think we are entitled to them without making very much effort. I do not think there is a country in the world where people can make a living with as little effort as in Canada. I notice the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) muttering something over there; I do not know what it is.

Mr. W.OOD:	The hon. member for St.
Paul's (Mr. Ross) the other day made a remark in which he emphasized some of the difficulties facing the city of Toronto. Well, Toronto has the highest tax rate of any city in Ontario. I know they are having some difficulties, but they enjoy more luxuries in that city than in other parts of the country, and I do not think they should object to paying for the privileges they enjoy. They want to get out from under their debt, but they want the rest of us to assume some portion of it. I had occasion to go through the records concerning the province of Ontario, and I found that Toronto had a per capita tax rate of S66.40. Next highest was the city from which the leader of the opposition comes, with $63.60. That might be a fairly good warning to the Canadian people; if that is the way he has left the city of Fort William, we should be very cautious about inviting him to administer the affairs of this country.

speechtext: I left Fort William some time ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The city of Brantford had a per capita tax rate of $46.70 while the rate in the township in which I live was $20. The hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. War-

The Address-Mr. Leclerc
ren) mentioned the fact that some of the rural municipalities have led the way in good financing. I would say that at least they have refrained from going into debt, and it might be a good thing if some of our cities would adopt the more frugal methods that are followed in some of these one-horse towns, as they are often called. If you are going into debt, you should assume the obligation of endeavouring to repay that debt. I agree with Mr. McCullagh in one thing, at least; I believe we can pay our debts if we really take steps toward that end, and we should see to it that we do not go further in debt. I agree with the policy of paying our way as we go.
Well, Mr. Speaker, since you have seen fit to give me the time, I am going to direct attention to how we spend our money. In 1937 we had a national income of $5,000,000,000, and how did we spend it? We spent about $1,000,000,000 for government, federal, provincial and municipal. Of that amount some $300,000,000 went for interest on our debts. We spent $135,000,000 for education, $100,000,000 for relief, $5S,000,000 for soldiers' pensions and $38,000,000 for old age pensions, of which over $28,000,000 was contributed by the federal government and a little over $9,000,000 by the provincial governments. We spent $35,000,000 on defence. The balance went for hospitalization, administration of justice and other servicesv
As I have said, we spent $1,000,000,000 for government. How did we spend the other $4,000,000,000? We spent about $1,000,000,000 for food; about $500,000,000 for clothing, which amounted to only about 13 cents per capita a day; about $300,000,000 for housing; about $200,000,000 for furniture, and $300,000,000 for fuel. In other words, we spent about $2,000,000,000 on food, clothing and shelter. This resume was taken from Toronto Saturday Night and was prepared by Mr. W. A. Kague. I am not going to be responsible for its accuracy, but I did check many of these figures with the Canada Year Book, and found them to be approximately correct.
As I have said, we spent $1,000,000,000 for government and $2,000,000,000 for food, clothing and shelter, leaving $2,000,000,000 to be accounted for, in connection with what might be termed non-essentials. How did we spend that money? In the first place we spent $300,000,000 on automobiles, some of which no doubt are quite necessary. We spent $125,000.000 for liquor, half of which of course returned to the revenue of the country. We spent $90,000,000 for tobacco; $45,000,000 for theatres, and $45,000,000 for other amusements,
including S25,000,000 for horse-racing, baseball and other games. We spent $150,000,000 for doctors and lawyers. I do not know how much the leader of the opposition 'got out of that, but I believe he would be better practising his profession than in endeavouring to try to cure the ills of the country.
There is one point to which I should like to draw attention, and that is that we spent $10,000,000 more on the church than we did on tobacco. We spent $100,000,000 on the church; $60,000,000 for books, magazines and newspapers, and $50,000,000 for telephone and telegraph services. We spent $100,000,000 on the tourist traffic, while at the same time $250,000,000 was spent on tourist travel in Canada. We pay to banks, insurance companies and brokerage and other financial services. We buy musical instruments, sporting goods and jewellery. We support the barber, and various other tradesmen.
But what I do say is this, that I believe we can assume the obligation which has been placed upon us. I do not think there is any short-cut to it except to get down to business. We may have to sacrifice some of these nonessentials, but I think any hon. member who will take the trouble to make a comparison with any other country of the world will find out that the Canadian people do enjoy a higher standard of living, higher possibly than that of any other group of people. As I have said, unfortunately we have the poor; they are always with us. It is our duty to do our bit towards trying to assist them to get back to the sober realities of life, even though this means sacrifice to ourselves.
I should like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for this extension of time. May I say in closing to the leader of the opposition-and it is described as His Majesty's Loyal Opposition: Be loyal to Canada. Be frank and truthful, and if you are going to tell some of the facts, tell all the facts. We know there are some unfortunate conditions, but I believe we should blend with them some of those fortunate things the people of Canada do enjoy.
Mr. JOSEPH H. LECLERC (Shefford) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I do not wish to trespass unduly on the valuable time of the house. I desire first of all to congratulate the hon. members who proposed and seconded the address on their excellent performance of this important task. My special congratulations go to the young and modest member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) who has done honour to his constituency. On behalf of my compatriots of Quebec province I am happy to offer him
The Address-Mr. Leclerc

my respectful homages and to salute in him a public man who is at the threshold of a promising career.
I also wish to offer my congratulations to the two ministers who have just recently joined the cabinet, as well as to the new leader of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition (Mr. Manion) to whom I wish a long tenure of office.
Mr. Speaker, the government deserves commendation for its constant efforts to re-establish normal conditions in this country. I am pleased to note the keen interest the King government is taking in the training of our youth. Once it is better understood and practically administered, the youth training plan will certainly prove very useful.
I am certain that the new trade agreement with the United States will prove of great benefit to the farmers of the eastern townships in the sale of their products, particularly maple sugar. On the whole, 1938 has not been too bad a year for agriculture; prices kept up satisfactorily until the end of the summer, 'but there is room for improvement. However, there is a dark side to the question; that is over-production of dairy products, particularly of butter. Although our exports in 1938 were practically at the same level as in 1937, we had in storage at the beginning of the present winter an abnormal quantity of butter which brought about a decline in price and afforded our opponents an opportunity to make political capital with the aid of unsound arguments.
In his speech of January 20, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman) said that the price of butter, in December last, was only 21 cents a pound, compared to 26 cents in December, 1935, and he ascribed that decline to our imports of last winter. Seeing that Tories use that argument from one end of the country to the other in order to mislead the farmers, let me, sir, give the actual facts. The hon. member for Carleton may be in good faith, but he evidently does not know anything about the subject because his statement is not borne out by the facts. It is true, as the hon. member said, that we imported last winter, from New Zealand and Australia, 4,271,373 pounds of butter. But does he know that, at that time, we were short of 10 million pounds for the ordinary needs of the country; that, as a result, the retail price of butter jumped to more than 40 cents a pound, and that a number of organizations of housewives in our large cities decided to boycott that product?
Imports are harmful when they hurt the producer; they are justified when they have

the effect of protecting the consumer. Had we not imported butter, last winter, who would have benefited by the high price, which would have jumped to 50 cents a pound and even higher? The farmers would certainly not have derived any benefit from it, for, during that period, butter production was at its lowest; speculators would then have reaped huge profits at the expense of consumers, and prices would have become prohibitive for the labouring classes.
Mr. Speaker, judging by the speech delivered by the hon. member for Carleton, it would appear that quite a number of members of this house do not have the slightest knowledge of dairying. If I may be permitted to use a financial term, I should say that in the case of butter the fiscal year ends with the month of April. At that time of the year, the stocks in storage are usually at their lowest. The year's production begins on May 1, when any large surplus may have a depressing influence upon the new butter-making season.
Mr. Speaker, in order to prove conclusively to the house and to the farmers of this country that the imports of last winter have not affected the prices now prevailing, I may say that on May 1, 1938, there were only 4,677,240 pounds of butter in storage in Canada, as compared with 6,125,243 pounds on the same date in 1937, when no imports had been made. The year 1938-39 thus began under the best possible conditions, there being only a minimum quantity of butter in storage and no imports having been made since that date. If the hon. member had seriously wanted to enlighten the electors of this country, he could easily have looked into the reasons for the drop in the price of butter since the beginning of this winter. The first of these reasons is to be found in the abundance of rain and in the excellent condition of pastures during the season of 1938 which have resulted in an increase of over 20 million pounds in the production of creamery butter, with no corresponding increase in consumption. The second lies in the high prices of butter during the winter of 1938, which caused a large number of people to speculate in the hope of reselling their butter at the top prices of last winter. It would be interesting to know the number of merchants, business men, professional men and others in our rural communities who have speculated in butter, and bought last June at 25 and 26 cents, thus holding prices above the export price at a time when we should have been shipping our surplus production. If it had not been for that speculative craze, the price of butter would have fluctuated normally. We would have exported our surplus production which

Standing Committees
has disturbed the market since the beginning of the winter, and the Christmas and New Year holidays would have been better enjoyed by the speculators. But they should feel happier at the thought that the money they have lost in speculation has fallen into the pockets of the farmers and buttressed the prices during the season of abundant production, which is better than the high prices in winter and low prices in summer which we had been getting from 1931 to 1934.
Mr. Speaker, while I have made clear the causes which have affected the market for that product during 1938, it does not necessarily follow that I am content with allowing the price of butter to find its own level, as dairying is the main branch of the farming industry in Canada, and the one on which the greatest number of Canadian farmers are dependent. That industry deserves more consideration than it has received in the past.
I am pleased to notice the interest w'hieh my fellow members, especially those from the eastern townships, are taking in that matter. But were I alone in promoting the interests of that industry and of the farmers who depend upon it, I would do it apart from eveiy political consideration. Liberalism is broad enough to allow its representatives to hold views which they consider in the general interest. I hope that before the end of this session the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will realize the necessity of creating an organization empowered to fix a minimum price for our dairy products and to export any surplus left over and above the country's requirements.
Following this brief analysis of the present situation of the dairy industry in this country, allow me. Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, to define my attitude on another burning question, the question of immigration, concerning which many petitions have been received. In spite of the deep sympathy we feel for certain persecuted peoples, we must remember that charity begins at home. We have enough unfortunates to help at home without opening our doors to those from abroad.
